instructions: For each pair, read both journeys as an observer under exactly these conditions and answer left, right, equal or neither, with an optional note. Do not open `hidden` until you have answered every pair: it holds the hypothesis and the engine's scores.

glossary.short: One sixtieth of an arcminute. The gaps in close double stars are measured in arcseconds.
Looking slightly to one side of a faint object, so its light falls on the more sensitive edge of your eye.
The circle of sky your binoculars show at once. Its width in degrees is printed on most binoculars.
A collapsed object whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape it.
The crowded, rounded swarm of stars at the center of a spiral galaxy.
A cool giant whose atmosphere is rich in carbon, which filters out blue light and makes it look deep red.
A pulsing supergiant that brightens and fades on a strict rhythm. The slower the rhythm, the more light it really gives off.
Close enough to the celestial pole that it never sets from your location, circling the pole all night.
The other star in a pair, usually the fainter one.
One of 88 official regions of the sky, each named after the old star figure inside it, such as Orion or Cygnus.
Two stars whose orbit we see edge-on, so they take turns passing in front of each other and the light dips.
The huge, thin sphere of old stars and globular clusters surrounding a galaxy's flat disk.
A dense ball of hundreds of thousands of very old stars, orbiting our galaxy far from its flat disk.
The second-lightest element. Stars make it by fusing hydrogen, and heavier stars later fuse it into carbon and oxygen.
The lightest and most common element, the main fuel stars burn for most of their lives.
The rarest, most luminous kind of supergiant: so bloated and unstable it sheds huge amounts of gas.
Several telescopes linked to act as one giant one, sharp enough to measure star sizes or split very close pairs.
A graph of a star's brightness over time, showing how it rises and falls.
The distance light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion km. It measures distance, not time.
The total light a star really gives off, however near or far it is. The Sun's is the usual yardstick.
The astronomer's brightness scale. Smaller numbers are brighter; each step of 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness.
The long, steady adult stage of a star's life, when it quietly fuses hydrogen in its core, as the Sun does now.
Our home galaxy, and the faint band of light it makes across the sky because we see its disk from inside.
A cloud of gas and dust in space. Some glow, some reflect starlight and some block the light behind them.
A loose family of stars born together from one cloud, usually a few hundred million years old or younger.
Two stars that only look close because they lie in nearly the same direction, at very different distances.
The tiny shift of a nearby star against far ones as Earth circles the Sun. The smaller the shift, the farther the star.
The glowing shell a dying Sun-like star puffs off. It has nothing to do with planets; early telescopes made them look like planets.
A star that swells and shrinks in a rhythm, getting brighter and fainter as it does.
A small, cool star lighter than the Sun. Such stars burn their fuel so slowly that they outlive every other kind.
An ageing star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to many times its old size, cooling to orange or red.
Starlight spread into its rainbow of colors. Dark or bright lines in it reveal a star's makeup, temperature and motion.
A galaxy shaped like a flat disk with curving arms of young stars and gas around a central bulge.
A rich patch of the Milky Way where we look through gaps in the dust into crowds of distant stars.
A cloud of gas and dust where new stars are forming right now.
A heavy star late in life, swollen to enormous size and pouring out thousands of times the Sun's light.
The explosion of a star, briefly outshining a whole galaxy of ordinary stars. Heavy stars end this way.
Light with shorter waves than violet, invisible to the eye. Hot stars pour out lots of it.
A star whose brightness changes, because it pulses, erupts, or is eclipsed by a partner.
The leftover core of a Sun-like star: about Earth's size but as heavy as the Sun, slowly cooling for billions of years.
Very energetic light, invisible to the eye, given off by gas at millions of degrees.

journeys.title: Where Cepheus Breaks the Records
journeys.drivingQuestion: How big, how bright and how far can a binocular target be?
journeys.hook: Each stop tonight is a record holder, extreme for a physical reason you can name.
journeys.story: Among the ordinary-looking stars hide some of the most extreme objects your eyes will ever catch. Tonight you visit them from VV Cephei to the Andromeda Galaxy, and every record has a reason.
journeys.payoff: Extremes are where physics shows its hand: the Andromeda Galaxy tops tonight's list, and its record, like all the others, has a cause you can name.
journeys.difficultyReason: η Cassiopeiae is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north-west, around Cepheus

stops.name: VV Cephei
stops.plainClass: red supergiant + blue-white star, eclipsing binary

getThere.text: Find Alderamin by eye, the brightest star of Cepheus, about 35° up in the north-west. From there, hop up about half a field of your 6.5° binoculars (4°) to VV Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Tonight is a tour of extremes, and the first record holder is VV Cephei, one of the largest stars within binocular reach.

card.question: How can an eclipse measure a star too distant to see as a disk?
card.glance: A modest orange star in Cepheus that shows no sign of being two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees north of the Garnet Star, so sweep between the two and compare them. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery, and its slow changes are too small to judge by eye.
card.understand: The star you see is a red supergiant, a heavyweight in the bloated last stage of its life, and a hot blue star circles it on an orbit we see nearly edge-on. Once every 20.3 years the giant swings in front of its partner and hides it for a long stretch. Knowing the blue star’s speed from its light, astronomers can treat the eclipse like a car passing behind a long wall: speed multiplied by time gives the length of the wall.
card.answer: The hidden star acts as a probe, and pacing out its passage behind the giant gives the giant’s width almost directly. Interferometers, which read its tiny disk, put it at hundreds of times the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: Its eclipses are among the longest known, the blue star staying hidden behind the giant for well over a year.
card.connect: Algol’s wink every few days and VV Cephei’s twenty-year eclipse are the same geometry, with only the size of the stars and their orbit changed.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Stay put: the Garnet Star is in the same view, below and to the left of VV Cephei.

stops.whyHere: William Herschel likened its color to a garnet, and it is the clearest proof in the sky that color is a star’s thermometer.
stops.transitionText: The Garnet Star and VV Cephei are red supergiants a few degrees apart, but only VV Cephei keeps a hot companion, which it passes in front of every 20 years.

card.question: How big can a star grow, and why does the Garnet Star glow so red?
card.glance: A deep orange-red point at the edge of the Milky Way in Cepheus, one of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: Start at Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, and look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. In binoculars its color leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus deepens it toward the gem it is named for.
card.understand: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white, and stars follow the same rule. At about 3,700 K the Garnet Star’s surface is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the star is visible from more than a thousand light-years away. A cool surface can only pour out that much light if it is enormous, and interferometers, which combine telescopes to measure its tiny disk, confirm it.
card.answer: It is a red supergiant, swollen to roughly a thousand times the Sun’s width near the end of its life, and its cool surface glows deep orange. Dust in front of it reddens it further, the way haze reddens a setting Sun.
card.wonder: Set it in the Sun’s place and its surface would lie far beyond the orbit of Mars, perhaps out toward Jupiter.
card.connect: A star this heavy will end as a supernova, scattering the elements it forged, as Betelgeuse in Orion will.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Sweep up about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°) to ρ Cassiopeiae, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae is a yellow hypergiant, a star at the very top of the power scale, and a lesson in how badly faintness can mislead. A star's weight decides its life story: heavy stars burn out in a few million years, light ones last for billions.
stops.transitionText: The Garnet Star is about 1,300–2,800 light-years away and ρ Cassiopeiae about 9,170 light-years, another long step outward.

card.question: How can a star you can barely see be one of the sky’s most powerful?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia that looks entirely ordinary.
card.see: Start at Caph, the western end of Cassiopeia’s W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to a faint yellowish star. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of NGC 7789 between them.
card.understand: Most stars that look bright are simply close, and ρ Cas is the opposite case. Astronomers fix its distance from the family of stars it travels with and measure its true width with interferometers, and together those give its real output. A star this extreme, roughly 40 times the Sun’s mass, lives in a brief, unstable late stage, and in 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.
card.answer: From about 9,000 light-years away, a star needs more than half a million times the Sun’s output to reach your eye at all, and ρ Cassiopeiae has it. The faint dot near Caph is one of the most luminous stars you can see.
card.wonder: That single outburst in 2000 shed gas weighing roughly 10,000 Earths.
card.connect: Power, not closeness, puts it in your sky: η Cassiopeiae, brighter to the eye, is only about 19 light-years away.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey 2 (POSS-II / UK Schmidt plates) · STScI / NASA; colour HiPS by CDS (Strasbourg), via the ESASky mirror; field reprojected by StarHop

image.caption: Survey photo of the binocular field around ρ Cassiopeiae, 4° wide; ρ Cassiopeiae is the star at the centre, between the four marks. North up, east left. A long photographic exposure, so it shows more stars and colour than binoculars do.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (18°) to the Andromeda Galaxy, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: The Andromeda Galaxy is the final record holder of the night. It is a whole other galaxy, and for most people the most distant thing they will ever see unaided.
stops.transitionText: The Andromeda Galaxy lies about 2,480,000 light-years away, about 270 times farther than ρ Cassiopeiae.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of M31 with its two bright companions, M32 just below the core and M110 to the upper right.

stops.name: η Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Sweep right about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°) to η Cassiopeiae, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: η Cassiopeiae is a near-twin of the Sun only 19 light-years away, which makes it a mirror held up to our own star.
stops.transitionText: Close on the sky, they are far apart in space, the Andromeda Galaxy about 2,480,000 light-years away and η Cassiopeiae about 19 light-years.

card.question: What would our Sun look like from a neighboring star?
card.glance: A pale yellow star in Cassiopeia’s W with a faint orange companion that steady, high-power binoculars can sometimes split.
card.see: η Cas sits between Schedar and γ Cas in the W. Its companion is only 13 arcseconds away and far fainter, so most hand-held binoculars show a single star. Brace 10× or larger binoculars on something solid and look for a tiny orange dot pressed against the yellow glare.
card.understand: The bright star is close to a twin of the Sun, slightly hotter, and its companion is a cooler, smaller orange dwarf. Observers have recorded the pair since 1779, and over those centuries the companion has swung a long way around its orbit. Kepler’s laws turn the size and period of an orbit into the mass that drives it, so this slow dance weighs both stars.
card.answer: Move the Sun out to 19 light-years and it would shine at about the brightness of η Cassiopeiae itself, a modest naked-eye star. Somewhere out there, an observer could be looking at our Sun as just another point in their sky.
card.wonder: Seen from η Cassiopeiae, our Sun would sit in the opposite part of the sky, close to the stars we call the Southern Cross.
card.connect: γ Cas, right beside it in the W and brighter to the eye, is nearly thirty times farther away.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the 1.5° field around η Cassiopeiae; bright stars appear as saturated disks, so sizes in the photo are not real sizes.

journeys.title: Perseus' Scattered Siblings
journeys.drivingQuestion: Are stars born alone, or do they have families?
journeys.hook: From tight young clusters to scattered families, tonight shows how star families age.
journeys.story: Stars are born in batches from a single cloud, then slowly drift apart. Tonight you meet families of different ages, from the Double Cluster (h Persei) to NGC 752, and watch the ties loosen.
journeys.payoff: From the close-knit family of the Double Cluster (h Persei) to the looser one of NGC 752, the pattern is clear: star families start tight and spread out with time.
journeys.difficultyReason: M103 is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north, around Perseus

stops.name: Double Cluster (h Persei)

getThere.text: Find Ruchbah by eye, a star of the W of Cassiopeia, about 65° up in the north-west. From there, hop up about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (8°) to the Double Cluster (h Persei).

stops.whyHere: We begin with the Double Cluster (h Persei), a family of stars that has not yet drifted apart.

card.question: Why do a few orange stars shine among the Double Cluster’s blue-white crowd?
card.glance: Two rich swarms of stars side by side in one view between Cassiopeia and Perseus, a naked-eye smudge from a dark site.
card.see: Sweep from Cassiopeia’s W toward Perseus and two glittering knots appear in one field, each crowded with dozens of points, the western one, h Persei, a little richer in the middle. Look for a few orange stars among the blue-white, especially toward the eastern cluster.
card.understand: Both clusters formed in the same burst of star birth, so all their stars share a birthday. Most are hot blue-white stars many times heavier than the Sun, and the orange points are the heaviest of all. Weight is destiny for a star: the more massive it is, the faster it burns, so those few have already raced to their last chapter.
card.answer: The orange stars were born with the rest, but being the heaviest they aged fastest and have swollen into red supergiants, cool on the surface and orange in color. Their ages, read from the supergiants alone, match the cluster’s, a neat cross-check.
card.wonder: They lie about 7,400 light-years away, more than ten times farther than the Pleiades, yet are still bright enough to see without binoculars.
card.connect: Its twin, χ Persei, sits half a degree east, born of the same cloud at the same time.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph framing both clusters, h Persei on the right and χ Persei on the left.

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the left about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (8°) to the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: The Owl Cluster is a young family with an open puzzle: is its brightest eye a member, or a star in front?
stops.transitionText: The Owl Cluster and the Double Cluster are young, rich families on the same spiral arm, both thousands of light-years away and only tens of millions of years old.

card.question: Does the Owl Cluster’s bright eye really belong to the cluster?
card.glance: Two bright “eyes” at one end of a small, elongated swarm in Cassiopeia, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other; the bright one is φ Cassiopeiae. A faint, slightly elongated spray trails away from them, and steady binoculars turn it into outstretched wings or arms.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,000 light-years away and only some 20 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life; if it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia’s parallax for φ Cas matches the cluster’s, but very bright stars are hard for Gaia to measure, and its speed toward us differs somewhat from older values.
card.answer: Probably, since the evidence leans toward membership, which would make the owl’s eye one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. The case is not closed, and that is part of the fun.
card.wonder: If φ Cas is a member, the light reaching you set out about 9,000 years ago.
card.connect: M103, a degree from Ruchbah, is a cluster whose stars clearly belong together.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of NGC 457 with its two bright "eyes" at the south-east end.

stops.name: M103

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: M103 is already in the same view, just right of the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster).

stops.whyHere: M103 is one of several young clusters strung along a spiral arm of the Milky Way in Cassiopeia. It is tonight's challenge, so give it a patient minute and skip it without guilt if it stays hidden.
stops.transitionText: The Owl Cluster and M103 are young families on the same spiral arm, a few degrees apart and at similar distances, which makes their different looks easy to compare.

card.question: Why is Cassiopeia so crowded with star clusters?
card.glance: A small, compact knot of faint stars with a few brighter points, a degree from Ruchbah in Cassiopeia.
card.see: Put Ruchbah at the edge of the field and look one degree east-north-east for a small hazy wedge with a few stars sparkling in it, a grainy patch rather than a spray. Glance around, because other faint knots share this part of the Milky Way.
card.understand: M103 is a young star family about 8,000 light-years away and some tens of millions of years old. Spiral arms are where galaxies make most of their stars, because gas piles up there like traffic slowing at a bend. Looking toward Cassiopeia we look along the Perseus arm, the next arm out from ours, so many young clusters overlap in one direction.
card.answer: Our line of sight runs along a star-forming arm, where clusters such as M103 were born in the same stretch of gas. Cassiopeia is crowded for the same reason a street looks crowded when you look straight down it.
card.wonder: Its light set out long before the first cities were built.
card.connect: NGC 663, a little to the east, is a bigger and richer sibling from the same stretch of the arm.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of M103, a small wedge-shaped cluster.

stops.name: Alpha Persei Cluster

getThere.text: Move up about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (20°), and the Alpha Persei Cluster is there, in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: The Alpha Persei Cluster is a young star family close enough that its members scatter across your entire binocular view.
stops.transitionText: The Alpha Persei Cluster is a young open cluster like M103, but about 2 times older, about 80–100 million years against 28–67 million years.

card.question: What does a star family look like from up close?
card.glance: A loose spray of bright blue-white stars around yellow-white Mirfak, filling the whole field.
card.see: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and dozens of blue-white stars spread around it in curving chains. It is too big for most telescopes to frame, so binoculars or the eye alone take it in whole.
card.understand: This is an open cluster, a family of stars born together from one cloud, and Gaia picks out its members by their shared motion, like spotting a family walking together through a crowd. Its age comes from a subtle clue: the lightest members slowly destroy the lithium inside them, so the line between stars that still have lithium and those that have lost it works like a clock. Here it reads about 90 million years.
card.answer: Like the Alpha Persei Cluster: at 566 light-years its members spread over several Moon widths, a spray only binoculars can frame. Farther away, the same family would shrink into a small knot.
card.wonder: This family was born while dinosaurs still had tens of millions of years left.
card.connect: The Double Cluster, more than ten times farther away, shows how small a star family looks from across the galaxy.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the Alpha Persei Cluster: bright blue-white stars scattered around Mirfak.

stops.name: NGC 752

getThere.text: Move left about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (19°), and NGC 752 is there, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: NGC 752 shows what time does to a family of stars. It is an old star family, over a billion years old, in the middle of falling apart.
stops.transitionText: NGC 752 is an open cluster like the Alpha Persei Cluster, but about 1.3 billion years old against 80–100 million years.

card.question: What is left of a star family after more than a billion years?
card.glance: A broad, even scatter of faint stars larger than the full Moon, next to the orange pair 56 Andromedae.
card.see: Start at the wide orange double 56 Andromedae in southern Andromeda and look just north-east for a large, loose patch of faint, similar stars. There is no bright center and no standout blue-white star, so let your eye relax over the whole field.
card.understand: In a young cluster the brightest stars are hot blue-white heavyweights, but here only stars a little heavier than the Sun remain in their steady adult life. That dividing line works as a clock, because the heavier a star, the sooner it leaves its adult phase, and here it reads about 1.34 billion years. Gaia counts about 440 members but only about 320 Suns’ worth of mass still bound together.
card.answer: Only the lighter members, a few new giants and a family coming loose at the seams. The galaxy’s tides have been pulling NGC 752 apart for over a billion years, and its stars are slowly mixing into the Milky Way.
card.wonder: This family is already about a tenth as old as the universe, and most clusters dissolve long before reaching such an age.
card.connect: NGC 7789 in Cassiopeia is a family of similar age, several times farther away and far richer.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of NGC 752, a loose sprinkle of stars wider than the full Moon.

journeys.title: Reading Cassiopeia Like a History Book
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight leave home?
journeys.hook: Looking farther means looking back in time, and each stop tonight shows older light.
journeys.story: Light is fast but not instant, so everything you see in the sky is already history. Each stop tonight shows older light than the last, from Capella out to the Andromeda Galaxy.
journeys.payoff: The light from the Andromeda Galaxy set out about 2.5 million years ago, the oldest of the night, and it reached your eye in the same moment as the far younger light of Capella.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Cassiopeia

stops.name: Capella

getThere.text: Find Capella by eye, the bright yellow star of Auriga, about 45° up in the north-east. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Every star you see is a message from the past, and the one from Capella has been on its way for about 43 years.

card.question: How can two giant stars hide inside a single point of light?
card.glance: The golden leader of Auriga, riding high on winter evenings.
card.see: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings, leading the pentagon of Auriga. Its creamy, slightly golden tint sits halfway between Rigel’s ice and Aldebaran’s orange. Just south of it lies the thin triangle of fainter stars called the Kids.
card.understand: The two stars circle each other every 104 days, so close that only interferometers, which combine several telescopes into one sharp eye, can separate them. Follow the orbit and the same laws that weigh the planets give the masses: about two and a half Suns each. Add each star’s measured size and temperature and something odd appears, because one already burns helium in its core, the fuel of a star’s later years, while its near-twin is only now swelling into a giant.
card.answer: Each giant is about ten times wider than the Sun, yet from 43 light-years their whole orbit shrinks to a speck that only an interferometer can open up.
card.wonder: A difference of a few percent in mass was enough to put two stars born together in different chapters of life.
card.connect: Next door in the Kids, a stranger pair hides one star inside a vast dark disk.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the Capella field.

stops.name: Mirfak

getThere.text: From Capella, slide up about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (19°) to Mirfak, in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: Mirfak is the brightest member of the Alpha Persei Cluster, a young star family that fits in one binocular view and shows two stages of life at once.
stops.transitionText: Mirfak lies about 506 light-years away, about 10 times farther than Capella.

card.question: Why is Mirfak yellower than the blue-white stars that surround it?
card.glance: The brightest star of Perseus, yellow-white and ringed in binoculars by a swarm of blue-white stars.
card.see: Aim at Mirfak, between Capella and Cassiopeia’s W, and the field fills with dozens of blue-white stars strung in curving chains, with Mirfak a shade yellower than the rest. Wide, low-power binoculars frame this cluster better than any telescope.
card.understand: An open cluster is a family of stars born together from one gas cloud, so its members share a birthday and a distance. That makes it a natural experiment in which the one big difference is how much mass each star started with. Heavy stars burn their fuel disproportionately fast, so the heaviest runs out of core hydrogen first and swells while its lighter siblings carry on.
card.answer: Mirfak started out the heaviest of the family, about seven times the Sun’s mass, so it has already swollen into a yellow supergiant while its siblings still shine blue-white. It managed all that in about 41 million years, a blink beside the Sun’s billions.
card.wonder: Mirfak and its siblings still travel through space together, a family that has stayed close for tens of millions of years.
card.connect: In the older Pleiades, stars as heavy as Mirfak have already burned out.

stops.name: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster)

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (14°) to Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster), in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Stock 2 sits beside the Double Cluster on the sky, and pairing the two shows how much depth a single sweep can hide.
stops.transitionText: From Mirfak at about 506 light-years the view reaches out to Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster) at about 1,210 light-years, about 2 times farther.

card.question: Are two clusters side by side in the sky really neighbors?
card.glance: A big, sprawling stick figure of stars in Cassiopeia, arms flexed, about two Moon widths across.
card.see: From the Double Cluster, nudge about two degrees north, and a large loose group fills much of the view; many observers trace a little body with flexed arms, the “Muscleman”. Use the widest field you have, because a telescope is too narrow for it.
card.understand: Gaia measures each member’s parallax and averages them, which pins down a cluster’s distance far better than any single star could. For Stock 2 it gives about 1,200 light-years, and for the Double Cluster over 7,000. The ages differ too: Stock 2 has lost its hottest blue stars, a sign of a few hundred million years, while the Double Cluster’s still blaze.
card.answer: These two are not: Stock 2 is about six times nearer and far older than the glittering pair beside it, proof that clusters touching on the sky can live in completely different parts of the galaxy.
card.wonder: Gaia found about 3,000 members here, a big family hiding in plain sight because it is so spread out.
card.connect: Swing back to the Double Cluster: the nearer family looks bigger and looser, the farther one smaller and denser.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (7°) to the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), still in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: The Owl Cluster is a young family with an open puzzle: is its brightest eye a member, or a star in front?
stops.transitionText: Stock 2 (Muscleman Cluster) is about 1,210 light-years away and the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster) about 9,130 light-years, another long step outward.

card.question: Does the Owl Cluster’s bright eye really belong to the cluster?
card.glance: Two bright “eyes” at one end of a small, elongated swarm in Cassiopeia, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other; the bright one is φ Cassiopeiae. A faint, slightly elongated spray trails away from them, and steady binoculars turn it into outstretched wings or arms.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,000 light-years away and only some 20 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life; if it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia’s parallax for φ Cas matches the cluster’s, but very bright stars are hard for Gaia to measure, and its speed toward us differs somewhat from older values.
card.answer: Probably, since the evidence leans toward membership, which would make the owl’s eye one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. The case is not closed, and that is part of the fun.
card.wonder: If φ Cas is a member, the light reaching you set out about 9,000 years ago.
card.connect: M103, a degree from Ruchbah, is a cluster whose stars clearly belong together.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (18°) to the Andromeda Galaxy, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: With the Andromeda Galaxy you reach deepest into the past. It is a whole other galaxy, and for most people the most distant thing they will ever see unaided.
stops.transitionText: The Andromeda Galaxy sits about 2,480,000 light-years away, about 270 times farther than the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), so its light has a longer road behind it.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment

journeys.title: How Extreme Can Cygnus Get?
journeys.drivingQuestion: What are the most extreme things you can see tonight?
journeys.hook: The sky's record holders are within binocular reach, and every record has a cause.
journeys.story: Among the ordinary-looking stars hide some of the most extreme objects your eyes will ever catch. Tonight you visit them from 61 Cygni to the Andromeda Galaxy, and every record has a reason.
journeys.payoff: From 61 Cygni to the Andromeda Galaxy, every record holder is extreme for a physical reason, and the remarkable thing is that ordinary binoculars reach them all.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Cygnus

stops.name: 61 Cygni

getThere.text: Find Deneb by eye, the tail of Cygnus the Swan, a corner of the Summer Triangle, about 40° up in the north-west. From there, hop up and to the left about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (8°) to 61 Cygni.

stops.whyHere: Tonight is a tour of extremes, and the first record holder is 61 Cygni, the first star whose distance was measured.

card.question: Which star first showed how far away the stars really are?
card.glance: A faint naked-eye star south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.see: Find 61 Cygni about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart, a lovely contrast with white Deneb, which lies well over a hundred times farther away.
card.understand: As Earth swings around the Sun, a nearby star shifts very slightly against the distant ones behind it, just as your thumb jumps when you close one eye and then the other. Friedrich Bessel picked 61 Cygni because it crept across the sky unusually fast, a hint that it was close, and in 1838 he caught that tiny yearly shift. The angle was about a third of an arcsecond, the width of a coin seen from across a city.
card.answer: 61 Cygni, about 11 light-years away. Turning that small angle into a distance showed for the first time that even a nearby star is so remote that its light takes over a decade to reach us.
card.wonder: It moves about 5 arcseconds a year, enough to cross a full Moon's width in roughly 350 years.
card.connect: Barnard's Star in Ophiuchus moves twice as fast, the sky's speed record.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Close-up survey photograph of the 61 Cygni pair; the two orange dwarfs are 32″ apart.

stops.name: Deneb

getThere.text: From 61 Cygni, slide down and to the right about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (8°) to Deneb, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: A star's brightness in the sky mixes two things, how much light it makes and how far away it is, and Deneb is where the two come apart most dramatically.
stops.transitionText: Brilliant Deneb and faint 61 Cygni share a constellation, yet the faint one is our close neighbor and the brilliant one lies over a hundred times farther off.

card.question: Why does the most powerful star of the Summer Triangle look the faintest?
card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, the swan's tail in Cygnus, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan, and the top of the Northern Cross. Sweep slowly around it and the field fills with countless faint stars, because here you are looking along the Milky Way; then glance back at Vega, which is plainly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away. Deneb is too far for a precise parallax, so its distance is still argued over, but the best estimate puts it around 2,600 light-years, roughly a hundred times farther. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star a hundred times farther must pour out ten thousand times more light just to keep up.
card.answer: Deneb only looks modest because it is so far away. It is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen to about 200 times the Sun's width and shining with something like 200,000 Suns, and even from that distance it nearly keeps pace with its neighbor.
card.wonder: If the best estimate is right, the light entering your eye tonight set out when Rome was still a small kingdom.
card.connect: Stars like Deneb do not stay white: the Garnet Star in Cepheus shows the red supergiant stage that lies ahead.

image.caption: Survey photograph of the rich Milky Way field around Deneb; the star itself is a saturated point.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (16°), and the Garnet Star is there, in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: William Herschel likened its color to a garnet, and it is the clearest proof in the sky that color is a star’s thermometer.
stops.transitionText: Deneb is about 203 times the Sun's radius across, and the Garnet Star about 590–1,300 times the Sun's radius.

card.question: How big can a star grow, and why does the Garnet Star glow so red?
card.glance: A deep orange-red point at the edge of the Milky Way in Cepheus, one of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: Start at Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, and look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. In binoculars its color leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus deepens it toward the gem it is named for.
card.understand: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white, and stars follow the same rule. At about 3,700 K the Garnet Star’s surface is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the star is visible from more than a thousand light-years away. A cool surface can only pour out that much light if it is enormous, and interferometers, which combine telescopes to measure its tiny disk, confirm it.
card.answer: It is a red supergiant, swollen to roughly a thousand times the Sun’s width near the end of its life, and its cool surface glows deep orange. Dust in front of it reddens it further, the way haze reddens a setting Sun.
card.wonder: Set it in the Sun’s place and its surface would lie far beyond the orbit of Mars, perhaps out toward Jupiter.
card.connect: A star this heavy will end as a supernova, scattering the elements it forged, as Betelgeuse in Orion will.

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Move up about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (17°), and ρ Cassiopeiae is there, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: ρ Cassiopeiae is a yellow hypergiant, a star at the very top of the power scale, and a lesson in how badly faintness can mislead. A star's weight decides its life story: heavy stars burn out in a few million years, light ones last for billions.
stops.transitionText: The Garnet Star is about 1,300–2,800 light-years away and ρ Cassiopeiae about 9,170 light-years, another long step outward.

card.question: How can a star you can barely see be one of the sky’s most powerful?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia that looks entirely ordinary.
card.see: Start at Caph, the western end of Cassiopeia’s W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to a faint yellowish star. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of NGC 7789 between them.
card.understand: Most stars that look bright are simply close, and ρ Cas is the opposite case. Astronomers fix its distance from the family of stars it travels with and measure its true width with interferometers, and together those give its real output. A star this extreme, roughly 40 times the Sun’s mass, lives in a brief, unstable late stage, and in 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.
card.answer: From about 9,000 light-years away, a star needs more than half a million times the Sun’s output to reach your eye at all, and ρ Cassiopeiae has it. The faint dot near Caph is one of the most luminous stars you can see.
card.wonder: That single outburst in 2000 shed gas weighing roughly 10,000 Earths.
card.connect: Power, not closeness, puts it in your sky: η Cassiopeiae, brighter to the eye, is only about 19 light-years away.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: From ρ Cassiopeiae, slide up about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (18°) to the Andromeda Galaxy, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: The Andromeda Galaxy is the final record holder of the night. It is a whole other galaxy, and for most people the most distant thing they will ever see unaided.
stops.transitionText: The Andromeda Galaxy sits about 2,480,000 light-years away, about 270 times farther than ρ Cassiopeiae, so its light has a longer road behind it.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.

For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

hidden.question: A journey mostly of clusters, nebulae and galaxies against one mostly of stars: which do you prefer?

conditions.message: Dark sky with the Moon down: every kind of journey is available.

journeys.title: Reading Hercules Like a History Book
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight leave home?
journeys.hook: The light in your binoculars left these stars in different centuries of our history.
journeys.story: Light is fast but not instant, so everything you see in the sky is already history. Each stop tonight shows older light than the last, from Rasalhague out to the Great Hercules Globular Cluster.
journeys.payoff: Every stop showed a different moment of the past, and the Great Hercules Globular Cluster reaches back furthest: its light has crossed empty space for about 24,000 years to meet you.
journeys.difficultyReason: R Coronae Borealis is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Hercules

stops.name: Rasalhague

getThere.text: Find Rasalhague by eye, the head of Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, about 65° up in the south. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Every star you see is a message from the past, and the one from Rasalhague has been on its way for about 49 years.

card.question: Can two stars side by side show both ends of the color scale?
card.glance: The white head of Ophiuchus, 5° east of orange Rasalgethi; together they make an easy color pair.
card.see: Swing between Rasalhague and Rasalgethi: white against orange-red, obvious even to the naked eye once you compare them. In binoculars the contrast deepens, and the two fit within one slow sweep.
card.understand: Rasalhague is hotter than the Sun, near 7,850 K, and spins so quickly that it is squashed at the poles. Telescopes that combine the light of several mirrors have measured that shape, and space photometry shows it also pulses gently. Rasalgethi, by contrast, is a cool, swollen red giant.
card.answer: Hot, white Rasalhague and cool, orange-red Rasalgethi sit just 5° apart, and the difference in tint is a direct reading of their temperatures.
card.wonder: Its light took under 50 years to arrive; Rasalgethi's took about seven times longer.
card.connect: Same patch of sky, opposite ends of the temperature scale.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey 2 (POSS-II / UK Schmidt plates) · STScI / NASA; colour HiPS by CDS (Strasbourg), via the ESASky mirror; field reprojected by StarHop

stops.name: Kornephoros

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (18°), and Kornephoros is there, in Hercules.

stops.whyHere: Kornephoros is no rarity, and that is what makes it useful: it shows the stage the Sun is heading for.
stops.transitionText: Rasalhague is about 49 light-years away and Kornephoros about 148 light-years, another long step outward.

card.question: What will the Sun look like when it grows old?
card.glance: A yellow 3rd-magnitude star marking Hercules's shoulder, about 10° south of the Keystone.
card.see: In binoculars Kornephoros is a clean yellow point about 10° south of the Keystone. Compare its tint with white Rasalhague farther to the south-east, and the yellow becomes obvious.
card.understand: Kornephoros has used up the hydrogen in its core and left the long, steady phase of life. With its core contracting and its outer layers expanding, it has swollen to about 17 times the Sun's width. Interferometers have measured its tiny disk directly, so that size is seen, not guessed.
card.answer: In several billion years, once its core hydrogen runs out, the Sun should swell into a yellow giant much like Kornephoros.
card.wonder: When the Sun reaches this stage, its swollen disk will fill a broad patch of Earth's sky.
card.connect: Red Rasalgethi shows a giant at a later, puffier stage.

stops.name: Kappa Herculis

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (7°) to Kappa Herculis, still in Hercules.

stops.whyHere: Splitting doubles is a skill, and κ Herculis shows how much your shaking hands are costing you.
stops.transitionText: From Kornephoros at about 148 light-years the view reaches out to Kappa Herculis at about 394 light-years, about 3 times farther.

card.question: How steady do your binoculars need to be to split a close pair?
card.glance: A yellow 5th-magnitude star with a 6th-magnitude companion 27″ away in Hercules: a test for steady 10× binoculars.
card.see: Brace your binoculars against a post or a wall and κ Her shows a yellow primary with a fainter companion 27″ to the north-north-east. Hand-held at 7×, the pair usually looks like one stretched star.
card.understand: The gap is fixed, so what changes is your instrument: magnification spreads the stars apart, and steadiness keeps them from smearing into one. Bracing helps as much as extra power. The primary is a yellow giant about 394 light-years away; whether the companion is truly tied to it is unsettled.
card.answer: Steady enough to hold 10× still: braced, 10× binoculars split the 27″ gap, while hand-held 7× shows only a stretched star.
card.wonder: Splitting it trains the same skill as Albireo, with a tighter gap.
card.connect: The wide doubles of Draco and Lyra make an easy comparison.

stops.name: R Coronae Borealis
stops.plainClass: yellow supergiant, fades behind clouds of soot

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (12°), and R Coronae Borealis is there, in Corona Borealis.

stops.whyHere: Most variable stars pulse, eclipse or explode; R Coronae Borealis has a stranger habit, disappearing now and then inside its own soot. This is the night's challenge, and if it will not show after a patient minute, move on.
stops.transitionText: R Coronae Borealis sits about 1,900–2,800 light-years away, about 6 times farther than Kappa Herculis, so its light has a longer road behind it.

card.question: How can a star vanish from view for months and then come back?
card.glance: At normal light, a 6th-magnitude star inside the Northern Crown's bowl; at other times, missing altogether.
card.see: Look inside the curve of Corona Borealis, about 2° north of δ CrB. At normal light R CrB is an easy binocular star, a little fainter than the Crown's faintest stars; if the spot is empty, the star is in a fade, and that is a real observation too.
card.understand: R CrB is a supergiant, a star swollen to enormous size, and an oddly built one, almost empty of hydrogen and rich in carbon. Now and then a puff of gas leaving its surface cools enough for that carbon to condense into soot, much as a candle flame blackens a cold spoon. When such a cloud forms on our side, the star sinks from 6th magnitude to as faint as 15th.
card.answer: It hides behind soot of its own making and stays hidden until the cloud drifts off and thins, which can take months or years. Its strange chemistry hints at an equally strange birth, perhaps two white dwarfs that merged into one swollen star.
card.wonder: At its deepest it is thousands of times fainter than normal, as if someone had drawn a curtain across a lamp.
card.connect: Three degrees away, T CrB waits to do the opposite: brighten without warning.

stops.name: Great Hercules Globular Cluster

getThere.text: Move up about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°), and the Great Hercules Globular Cluster is there, in Hercules.

stops.whyHere: With the Great Hercules Globular Cluster you reach deepest into the past. Most stars live in the Milky Way's flat disk, but its oldest families orbit in a vast halo around it, and M13 is the grandest of them in northern skies.
stops.transitionText: The Great Hercules Globular Cluster lies about 24,200 light-years away, about 10 times farther than R Coronae Borealis.

card.question: What does a city of half a million ancient stars look like from here?
card.glance: A small, round, soft glow on the west side of the Hercules Keystone, brighter toward its middle.
card.see: Find the four-star Keystone of Hercules. About a third of the way from η to ζ Herculis sits a fuzzy ball that is clearly not a star, brightening toward its center; beside a star of similar brightness, one is a point and the other a cloud.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight ball of stars born together when the Milky Way was young. M13 packs roughly half a million Suns' worth of them into about 120 light-years, a space that around the Sun holds only a few thousand stars. Its stars are poor in iron and the other heavy elements, so they must have formed before many generations of stars had lived and died.
card.answer: From here it is a soft, round glow, yet it holds about half a million stars some 12 billion years old. On a planet near its core, the night sky would be crowded with stars far brighter than any we see.
card.wonder: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message about humanity toward M13, and it will need roughly 24,000 years to arrive.
card.connect: M92, Hercules's second globular, looks smaller but is even older and poorer in heavy elements.

journeys.title: Serpens' Cradles and Graves
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where do stars come from, and how do they end?
journeys.hook: Stars are born, grow old and die, and tonight you can see all three in a few sweeps.
journeys.story: Nothing in a star's life is wasted. The gas a dying star returns to space becomes the next generation, and tonight's stops follow that cycle from start to finish.
journeys.payoff: From the Omega Nebula to Tarazed, nothing in a star's life is wasted: what a dying star gives back becomes new stars and planets, and some of it, long ago, became us.
journeys.difficultyReason: Dumbbell Nebula is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Serpens

stops.name: Omega Nebula
stops.plainClass: glowing gas cloud where stars form

getThere.text: Find Sabik by eye in Ophiuchus, about 35° up in the south. From there, hop left about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°) to the Omega Nebula.

stops.whyHere: A star's life begins in cold gas, so that is where we start: the Omega Nebula is a nursery where new stars are still taking shape.

card.question: What does a star nursery less than a million years old look like?
card.glance: A short, bright bar of gray light with a faint hook at one end.
card.see: Sweep less than half a binocular field north of the Sagittarius Star Cloud, M24. Look for a small elongated glow, brighter than you expect, like a chalk streak; under a dark sky a fainter curl appears at one end, giving the swan or check-mark shape, and a nebula filter helps.
card.understand: Behind the bright bar sits a cluster of very massive newborn stars, mostly hidden by dust. Their ultraviolet light makes the surrounding hydrogen glow so intensely that the patch looks almost sharp-edged even in binoculars. Its age comes from a clever clock: several heavy stars have already been flung out by close encounters, and tracing their flight backward shows how recently they left.
card.answer: It looks like the Omega, a bright, sharp-edged bar of glowing gas lit by massive stars still hidden in dust, all less than a million years old, a nursery with the lights just switched on.
card.wonder: Stars this heavy live only a few million years, so this whole display is a brief flash in the Galaxy's history.
card.connect: M18, just south, is a family from the same arm that lost its cloud long ago.

image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: VST photograph: pink hydrogen and dark dust swirls around the bright bar.

stops.name: Eagle Nebula
stops.plainClass: glowing gas cloud where stars form

getThere.text: Stay put: the Eagle Nebula is in the same view, above and to the right of the Omega Nebula.

stops.whyHere: Star birth is not a gentle affair, and the Eagle Nebula, home of the Pillars of Creation, shows newborn stars eating away their own birth cloud.
stops.transitionText: A cloud like the Omega Nebula collapses into a nest of newborn stars like the Eagle Nebula, and that is where a star's life begins.

card.question: How do newborn stars destroy the cloud that made them?
card.glance: A small, bright scatter of stars wrapped in a faint haze, north of the Sagittarius Star Cloud.
card.see: Sweep north from the Sagittarius Star Cloud past M17 into Serpens. M16 shows as a tight scatter of a dozen or so stars in a soft glow, and averted vision under a dark sky brings out a dim haze, brighter on one side; the pillars themselves are far too small and faint for binoculars.
card.understand: The cluster is a few million years old, and its hottest stars flood the cloud with ultraviolet light, making the gas glow and slowly boiling it away. Dense knots resist longest and are left standing as dark columns, like sandcastle towers holding out as the tide flattens the beach. Hubble photographed them in 1995 and again in 2014, and the second image showed gas streaming off their surfaces.
card.answer: They do it with light, their ultraviolet glare boiling the gas away until only the densest knots survive as the Pillars of Creation, and even those are fraying. Stars still form inside them, racing to finish before their cradle is gone.
card.wonder: The tallest pillar is about five light-years long, more than the distance from the Sun to the nearest star.
card.connect: M17, its southern neighbor, is an even younger nursery, brighter in binoculars.

image.credit: ESO
image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: ESO optical mosaic: the cluster inside red hydrogen, with the dark pillars near the center.

stops.name: IC 4756

getThere.text: From the Eagle Nebula, slide up about three fields of your 6.5° binoculars (20°) to IC 4756, still in Serpens.

stops.whyHere: Most clusters dissolve long before they reach a billion years, so IC 4756, still together after nearly that long, is a survivor worth meeting.
stops.transitionText: If the Eagle Nebula is one chapter of a star's life, IC 4756 is the page you turn to after it.

card.question: Can a family of stars survive for nearly a billion years?
card.glance: A large, loose cloud of faint stars, a full degree across, that wants low power and a wide field.
card.see: From θ Serpentis, at the tip of the snake's tail, sweep about four degrees west. IC 4756 is a broad scatter of faint stars over two full-Moon widths whose edges blend into the Milky Way, so let your eyes find the slightly denser middle; NGC 6633 sits just across the border in Ophiuchus.
card.understand: Every time a cluster passes a giant gas cloud or feels the Galaxy's tides, a few stars are tugged away, so most families dissolve within a few hundred million years. IC 4756's heaviest stars are long gone, and a handful of members are now yellow and orange giants. It survived because it was born rich enough for its own gravity to hold on.
card.answer: A rich one can, and IC 4756, about 840 million years old, still holds over 700 members, thinned but together.
card.wonder: If the Sun's life so far were one day, this family was born about four hours ago.
card.connect: NGC 6633, just west, is a neighbor of similar age.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the broad, loose cluster.

stops.name: Tarazed

getThere.text: From IC 4756, slide left about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (17°) to Tarazed, in Aquila.

stops.whyHere: Tarazed, an orange giant, carries the life story to its latest stage tonight. Stars that look like a set often are not, and Tarazed beside Altair is one of the clearest cases.
stops.transitionText: Stars like those in IC 4756 eventually swell into giants, and Tarazed has already made that change.

card.question: Is Altair's orange neighbor really its neighbor?
card.glance: The orange star 2° north-north-west of Altair in Aquila; the color contrast in binoculars is obvious.
card.see: Put Altair and Tarazed in one field: crisp white against warm orange, about 2° apart. They look like a matched set, which makes the truth more surprising.
card.understand: Tarazed is a bright giant about 95 times wider than the Sun, some 400 light-years away. Altair is a modest star only 17 light-years off. Seen from the side, the two would be nowhere near each other; they merely line up from where we stand.
card.answer: Tarazed lies more than 20 times farther away than Altair and only looks comparable because it is a giant.
card.wonder: Their light set out at very different times: Altair's about 17 years ago, Tarazed's around four centuries ago.
card.connect: Albireo plays a similar trick of perspective.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey 2 (POSS-II / UK Schmidt plates) · STScI / NASA; colour HiPS by CDS (Strasbourg), via the ESASky mirror; field reprojected by StarHop
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photo of the binocular field around Tarazed, 4° wide; Tarazed is the star at the centre, between the four marks. North up, east left. A long photographic exposure, so it shows more stars and colour than binoculars do.

stops.name: Dumbbell Nebula

getThere.text: From Tarazed, slide up and to the left about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (13°) to the Dumbbell Nebula, in Vulpecula.

stops.whyHere: Most dying stars are too small or faint for binoculars, but the Dumbbell is close and large enough that you can see the shape of one star's last breath. When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.
stops.transitionText: The Dumbbell Nebula is a giant at the very end, giving its gas back to space.

card.question: Where is the easiest place to see how a Sun-like star dies?
card.glance: A small gray patch, clearly larger than any star, sometimes with a hint of a pinched apple-core shape.
card.see: Find the little arrow of Sagitta below Albireo, then move about 3° north of its tip star, γ Sagittae, into Vulpecula. M27 is a small, faint gray smudge; brace the binoculars and look slightly to one side, and on a dark night it turns squarish or hourglass-shaped.
card.understand: A star once like the Sun swelled into a giant and let its outer layers drift away, and its bare, extremely hot core now makes that gas glow like a neon sign. The outer shells are expanding at about 30 kilometers per second, and dividing the shell's size by that speed gives an age of roughly ten thousand years. Within tens of thousands more the gas will fade into space, carrying elements made inside the star.
card.answer: The Dumbbell may be the best place of all: a Sun-like star's shed layers, lit by its bare core and close enough, about 1,270 light-years, to show their shape in binoculars.
card.wonder: Its outer gas moves fast enough to cross the United States in under three minutes, yet from here the shape will look unchanged for your whole lifetime.
card.connect: Heavier stars go out violently; the Veil in Cygnus is the wreck of such an explosion.

image.credit: ESO / I. Appenzeller, W. Seifert, O. Stahl, M. Zamani
image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: Large-telescope composite: colors and the full hourglass the eye cannot see in binoculars.

hidden.question: A journey mostly of clusters, nebulae and galaxies against one mostly of stars: which do you prefer?
contrasts: challenge stop on the left only

conditions.message: The Moon is 47% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 24° from it; it sets at 23:12.

journeys.title: How Extreme Can Andromeda Get?
journeys.drivingQuestion: How big, how bright and how far can a binocular target be?
journeys.hook: Some of the most extreme objects in the galaxy hide among ordinary-looking stars.
journeys.story: Extremes are where physics shows its hand most clearly. Starting with Deneb, each stop holds a record, and each record has a cause you can name.
journeys.payoff: The most extreme sight of the night was the Andromeda Galaxy, and none of the records was an accident: each came from mass, age or sheer distance.
journeys.difficultyReason: Caroline's Rose is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Andromeda

stops.name: Deneb

getThere.text: Find Deneb by eye, the tail of Cygnus the Swan, a corner of the Summer Triangle, nearly overhead. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Tonight is a tour of extremes, and the first record holder is Deneb, by far the most luminous and most distant of the Summer Triangle stars.

card.question: Why does the most powerful star of the Summer Triangle look the faintest?
card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, the swan's tail in Cygnus, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan, and the top of the Northern Cross. Sweep slowly around it and the field fills with countless faint stars, because here you are looking along the Milky Way; then glance back at Vega, which is plainly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away. Deneb is too far for a precise parallax, so its distance is still argued over, but the best estimate puts it around 2,600 light-years, roughly a hundred times farther. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star a hundred times farther must pour out ten thousand times more light just to keep up.
card.answer: Deneb only looks modest because it is so far away. It is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen to about 200 times the Sun's width and shining with something like 200,000 Suns, and even from that distance it nearly keeps pace with its neighbor.
card.wonder: If the best estimate is right, the light entering your eye tonight set out when Rome was still a small kingdom.
card.connect: Stars like Deneb do not stay white: the Garnet Star in Cepheus shows the red supergiant stage that lies ahead.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the rich Milky Way field around Deneb; the star itself is a saturated point.

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: From Deneb, slide right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (16°) to the Garnet Star, in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: William Herschel likened its color to a garnet, and it is the clearest proof in the sky that color is a star’s thermometer.
stops.transitionText: Both are points of light, but the Garnet Star is about 5 times larger than Deneb.

card.question: How big can a star grow, and why does the Garnet Star glow so red?
card.glance: A deep orange-red point at the edge of the Milky Way in Cepheus, one of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: Start at Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, and look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. In binoculars its color leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus deepens it toward the gem it is named for.
card.understand: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white, and stars follow the same rule. At about 3,700 K the Garnet Star’s surface is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the star is visible from more than a thousand light-years away. A cool surface can only pour out that much light if it is enormous, and interferometers, which combine telescopes to measure its tiny disk, confirm it.
card.answer: It is a red supergiant, swollen to roughly a thousand times the Sun’s width near the end of its life, and its cool surface glows deep orange. Dust in front of it reddens it further, the way haze reddens a setting Sun.
card.wonder: Set it in the Sun’s place and its surface would lie far beyond the orbit of Mars, perhaps out toward Jupiter.
card.connect: A star this heavy will end as a supernova, scattering the elements it forged, as Betelgeuse in Orion will.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the 3.7° field around the Garnet Star; bright stars appear as saturated disks, so sizes in the photo are not real sizes.

stops.name: Caroline's Rose

getThere.text: From the Garnet Star, slide right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (18°) to Caroline's Rose, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Caroline’s Rose is an old and very rich family, in which over a billion years of aging have turned the brightest stars into giants. A star's weight decides its life story: heavy stars burn out in a few million years, light ones last for billions.
stops.transitionText: Caroline's Rose sits about 6,420 light-years away, about 5 times farther than the Garnet Star, so its light has a longer road behind it.

card.question: What does a star family look like after 1.6 billion years?
card.glance: A round, even, misty glow about half the Moon’s width, midway between ρ and σ Cassiopeiae.
card.see: From Caph, the end of Cassiopeia’s W, move about three degrees south-west to the faint pair ρ and σ Cassiopeiae; the cluster sits midway between them. In binoculars it is a soft, uniform patch, grainy under a dark sky, and the rose-petal pattern needs a telescope.
card.understand: NGC 7789 is roughly 1.6 billion years old, so its hot blue stars burned out long ago, and its brightest members now are stars a bit heavier than the Sun that have swollen into giants. It is also unusually massive: Gaia counts more than 4,000 members, the heaviest open cluster within about 7,000 light-years. Most families dissolve long before this age, and sheer mass is what has held this one together.
card.answer: It looks misty and even, a soft glow of yellow and orange giants among thousands of fainter stars. Time has dimmed its sparkle but not yet scattered the family.
card.wonder: Caroline Herschel found it in 1783 while sweeping the sky for comets with a small telescope.
card.connect: M52, a few degrees away, is the young, sparkling version.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of Caroline's Rose: thousands of faint stars with dark lanes like petals.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: From Caroline's Rose, slide right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (17°) to the Andromeda Galaxy, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: The last champion of the night is the Andromeda Galaxy, a spiral galaxy. It is a whole other galaxy, and for most people the most distant thing they will ever see unaided.
stops.transitionText: The Andromeda Galaxy spans about 128,000 light-years, about 4,300 times larger than Caroline's Rose.

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of M31 with its two bright companions, M32 just below the core and M110 to the upper right.

stops.name: υ Andromedae

getThere.text: Move down about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (10°), and υ Andromedae is there, still in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: υ Andromedae was the first Sun-like star found with more than one planet, the point where single discoveries turned into whole planetary systems.
stops.transitionText: Close on the sky, they are far apart in space, the Andromeda Galaxy about 2,480,000 light-years away and υ Andromedae about 44 light-years.

card.question: Can another sun hold a whole family of planets, not just one?
card.glance: A modest yellow-white star in Andromeda, a few binocular fields from the Andromeda Galaxy.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, move about eight degrees north-east to a modest yellow-white point. Its planets are invisible, but sweep west and the soft glow of the Andromeda Galaxy drifts into view.
card.understand: Like 51 Pegasi, the star wobbles toward and away from us, but its wobble is a tangle, as if several hands were tugging at once. Untangling it is like picking the separate notes out of a chord: one tug repeats in under five days, another about every eight months, a third about every three and a half years. Each rhythm is a planet, and the strength of each tug gives its mass.
card.answer: It can, and υ Andromedae was the first Sun-like star shown to: its wobble resolves into three giant planets on very different orbits. From then on, the Sun was no longer the only Sun-like star known to keep a family.
card.wonder: The star is a little hotter and larger than the Sun, so its comfortable zone for liquid water lies farther out than Earth’s orbit.
card.connect: One family of worlds 44 light-years away; a few binocular fields west, the Andromeda Galaxy holds hundreds of billions of suns.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment

journeys.title: Cygnus' Unlikely Twins
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do neighbors in the sky turn out to be so different?
journeys.hook: Stars that pass for twins can be strangers, and one hidden fact gives them away.
journeys.story: Looks deceive in the sky as much as anywhere. Starting at Deneb, you compare neighbors that seem alike and find the one difference that gave them such different lives.
journeys.payoff: What your eye sees, color and brightness, is only the surface; underneath, each look-alike pair differed in temperature, age, distance or mass, and that difference shaped their lives.
journeys.difficultyReason: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Cygnus

stops.name: Deneb

getThere.text: Find Deneb by eye, the tail of Cygnus the Swan, a corner of the Summer Triangle, nearly overhead. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Tonight's stars look alike at first and lead very different lives, so take in the color and brightness of Deneb, because both can mislead.

card.question: Why does the most powerful star of the Summer Triangle look the faintest?
card.glance: The faintest corner of the Summer Triangle, the swan's tail in Cygnus, set in a rich Milky Way field.
card.see: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus, the swan, and the top of the Northern Cross. Sweep slowly around it and the field fills with countless faint stars, because here you are looking along the Milky Way; then glance back at Vega, which is plainly brighter to the eye.
card.understand: Vega is about 25 light-years away. Deneb is too far for a precise parallax, so its distance is still argued over, but the best estimate puts it around 2,600 light-years, roughly a hundred times farther. Light thins out with the square of distance, so a star a hundred times farther must pour out ten thousand times more light just to keep up.
card.answer: Deneb only looks modest because it is so far away. It is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen to about 200 times the Sun's width and shining with something like 200,000 Suns, and even from that distance it nearly keeps pace with its neighbor.
card.wonder: If the best estimate is right, the light entering your eye tonight set out when Rome was still a small kingdom.
card.connect: Stars like Deneb do not stay white: the Garnet Star in Cepheus shows the red supergiant stage that lies ahead.
