image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the rich Milky Way field around Deneb; the star itself is a saturated point.

stops.name: 61 Cygni

getThere.text: Move up and to the left about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (8°), and 61 Cygni is there, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: For centuries nobody knew whether the stars lay just beyond the planets or unimaginably far, and this faint orange pair in Cygnus settled it.
stops.transitionText: Brilliant Deneb and faint 61 Cygni share a constellation, yet the faint one is our close neighbor and the brilliant one lies over a hundred times farther off.

card.question: Which star first showed how far away the stars really are?
card.glance: A faint naked-eye star south-east of Deneb; binoculars split it into two matched orange stars.
card.see: Find 61 Cygni about 8° south-east of Deneb, 1.7° west-north-west of τ Cygni. In 10× binoculars it splits into two warm orange points 32″ apart, a lovely contrast with white Deneb, which lies well over a hundred times farther away.
card.understand: As Earth swings around the Sun, a nearby star shifts very slightly against the distant ones behind it, just as your thumb jumps when you close one eye and then the other. Friedrich Bessel picked 61 Cygni because it crept across the sky unusually fast, a hint that it was close, and in 1838 he caught that tiny yearly shift. The angle was about a third of an arcsecond, the width of a coin seen from across a city.
card.answer: 61 Cygni, about 11 light-years away. Turning that small angle into a distance showed for the first time that even a nearby star is so remote that its light takes over a decade to reach us.
card.wonder: It moves about 5 arcseconds a year, enough to cross a full Moon's width in roughly 350 years.
card.connect: Barnard's Star in Ophiuchus moves twice as fast, the sky's speed record.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Close-up survey photograph of the 61 Cygni pair; the two orange dwarfs are 32″ apart.

stops.name: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868)

getThere.text: Sweep down about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (14°) to Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868), still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Most heavy stars end their lives out of sight, but here in the swan's neck is one of the first places where astronomers became sure black holes are real. It is tonight's challenge, so give it a patient minute and skip it without guilt if it stays hidden.
stops.transitionText: How bright a star looks depends on its distance too, and in truth Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) is about 2,800,000 times more luminous than 61 Cygni.

card.question: Can you see a star that is orbiting a black hole?
card.glance: A 9th-magnitude star half a degree from η Cygni in the swan's neck: unremarkable, unforgettable once you know.
card.see: Center η Cygni, midway along the swan's neck. About 0.4° to the east-north-east, less than a Moon's width away, a 9th-magnitude star slightly brighter than its neighbors is HDE 226868, and nothing about it looks special.
card.understand: This blue supergiant, about 40 times the Sun's mass, whips around an unseen partner every 5.6 days. Weighing the partner uses the same trick as weighing planets: measure how fast and how far the visible star swings to and fro, and gravity tells you what must be pulling it. In 2021 radio measurements pinned down the distance, and the partner came out at about 21 Suns while giving off no starlight at all.
card.answer: You are looking at one. An object that heavy which gives off no light of its own can only be a black hole, the collapsed core of a massive star, and gas torn from the supergiant glows in X-rays as it spirals in.
card.wonder: The light you see set off over seven thousand years ago, before writing was invented.
card.connect: The Veil Nebula shows the other way a heavy star can end: blown apart.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey 2 (POSS-II / UK Schmidt plates) · STScI / NASA; colour HiPS by CDS (Strasbourg), via the ESASky mirror; field reprojected by StarHop

stops.name: Albireo

getThere.text: From Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868), slide down and to the left about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (9°) to Albireo, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Albireo is the sky's most beautiful color contrast, gold beside blue, and that contrast turns out to be a thermometer you can read from your backyard.
stops.transitionText: Albireo is about 270 times less luminous than Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868), whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.question: Can you really read a star's temperature from its color?
card.glance: The swan's head in Cygnus, roughly halfway from Vega to Altair; steady binoculars split it into gold and blue.
card.see: Albireo marks the head of the swan, at the foot of the Northern Cross. Brace your binoculars on something solid and at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white spark beside it, 34″ away; if the split is hard, let the image drift and watch for the blue point trailing behind.
card.understand: Think of an electric stove ring as it heats: first dull red, then orange, and, if it could get hot enough, white and then blue. Stars are glowing balls of gas and follow the same rule. Their spectra pin down the numbers: the gold star is a cool giant near 4,400 K, the blue one about 13,000 K.
card.answer: You can, and Albireo proves it: the golden star is only about a third as hot as its blue companion, and your eye registers that gap as color. Every tint you notice tonight is a surface temperature read across hundreds of light-years.
card.wonder: For a century Albireo was the textbook orbiting pair; precise Gaia-era motions now suggest two siblings born together and slowly drifting apart.
card.connect: The Double-Double near Vega shows pairs that truly do orbit each other.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph centered on Albireo; the gold and blue stars merge into one saturated blob at this scale.

stops.name: Vega

getThere.text: From Albireo, slide right about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (16°) to Vega, in Lyra.

stops.whyHere: With Vega, a white star, the night's last pair of look-alikes is complete. Before a star can look strange, you need a normal one to measure it against, and Vega, bright and close, is the sky's classic yardstick.
stops.transitionText: Rank them by real output rather than by eye and Albireo gives about 1,560 times the Sun's light while Vega gives about 51 times the Sun's light.

card.question: What does an ordinary star look like in the long, calm prime of its life?
card.glance: The brilliant blue-white star almost overhead on summer evenings, the brightest corner of the Summer Triangle.
card.see: Vega is the jewel of the small constellation Lyra and the first star to appear overhead as the summer sky darkens. In binoculars it becomes a hard white spark ringed by faint stars your eyes alone would miss, with the Double-Double a short hop to the north-east and Lyra's little parallelogram hanging just below.
card.understand: Like the Sun, Vega is a main-sequence star, which simply means it is in the long, steady middle of life, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. It carries a little over twice the Sun's mass, and that extra weight squeezes the core harder, so the fire runs hotter and faster. You can read the result in its color: a surface near 9,500 K glows blue-white.
card.answer: It looks like Vega, steady, white and unremarkable in the best sense, though as a heavier star it spends its fuel lavishly and, at about 700 million years, is already well into a life far shorter than the Sun's.
card.wonder: A disk of dust about a thousand times the Earth–Sun distance across surrounds Vega, and Webb and Hubble found it so smooth that any planets hiding there must be small.
card.connect: Deneb, the Triangle's faintest corner, looks humbler than Vega but lies about a hundred times farther away.

journeys.title: Old Light over Boötes
journeys.drivingQuestion: When did tonight's starlight leave home?
journeys.hook: Looking farther means looking back in time, and each stop tonight shows older light.
journeys.story: The light entering your binoculars set out long before you looked up, and from each stop at a different time. Read the night like a calendar, starting with Arcturus, the freshest light.
journeys.payoff: The light from the Great Hercules Globular Cluster set out about 24,000 years ago, the oldest of the night, and it reached your eye in the same moment as the far younger light of Arcturus.
journeys.difficultyReason: R Coronae Borealis is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north-east, around Boötes

stops.name: Arcturus

getThere.text: Find Arcturus by eye, the bright orange star of Boötes, about 45° up in the east; follow the arc of the Big Dipper’s handle to it. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The light you see from Arcturus left it around 1990, and each stop after it shows older light still.

card.question: What will the Sun look like in old age?
card.glance: The brightest star of spring, a strong orange-gold light in Boötes at the end of the curve you follow from the Big Dipper’s handle.
card.see: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle away from the bowl to the first bright star, Arcturus, the brightest in Boötes. Its orange-gold is obvious in binoculars. Carry the same curve on to blue-white Spica and compare.
card.understand: Arcturus weighs about the same as the Sun but is billions of years older, and it has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 25 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 4,300 K, yet all that glowing surface makes it shine about 200 times as brightly as the Sun. It is also poor in heavy elements and crosses our sky fast, at about 122 kilometers per second, the mark of a visitor from the galaxy’s older, thicker disk.
card.answer: In billions of years the Sun will look much like Arcturus does tonight, an orange-gold giant with a cooler surface but far more light.
card.wonder: In 1933 its starlight switched on the lights of the Chicago World’s Fair.
card.connect: A star ten times heavier, Spica, will end far more violently.

stops.name: Izar

getThere.text: From Arcturus, slide left about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (10°) to Izar, still in Boötes.

stops.whyHere: Izar looks like a fainter copy of nearby Arcturus, the same orange in a smaller dose. A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light gets in one year of travel.
stops.transitionText: Izar lies about 203 light-years away, about 6 times farther than Arcturus.

card.question: Is Izar just a fainter Arcturus?
card.glance: An orange star in Boötes, single in binoculars, though telescopes reveal a lovely color pair.
card.see: In binoculars Izar is orange, like a dimmer copy of Arcturus ten degrees away in the kite of Boötes. Its blue-white companion is too close for binoculars.
card.understand: Izar lies about 200 light-years away, five or six times farther than Arcturus, though the parallax measurements disagree a little. Light spreads out as it travels, over an area that grows with the square of the distance, so from that far it would need around thirty times Arcturus’s output just to look as bright. It looks dimmer, but not by nearly that much.
card.answer: Izar is no lesser copy, since it must pour out roughly three times as much light as Arcturus to look even this bright from so far away.
card.wonder: Through a telescope its tiny companion looks blue against the orange primary, one reason it is nicknamed ‘the most beautiful’.
card.connect: δ and μ Boötis, nearby, are wide doubles your binoculars can split.

stops.name: ν¹ & ν² Boötis

getThere.text: Sweep left about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (17°) to ν¹ & ν² Boötis, still in Boötes.

stops.whyHere: ν Boötis looks like the best-matched pair in Boötes, two stars of equal brightness side by side.
stops.transitionText: From Izar at about 203 light-years the view reaches out to ν¹ & ν² Boötis at about 974 light-years, about 5 times farther.

card.question: Is the matched pair of ν Boötis a real couple?
card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes, one orange and one white.
card.see: Start at Nekkar, the star at the top of the kite of Boötes, and sweep east. Binoculars show orange ν¹ and white ν² side by side, nearly equal in brightness.
card.understand: Gaia settles it by parallax, each star's tiny shift as Earth circles the Sun. Those shifts put ν¹, an orange giant, nearly 1,000 light-years away, and ν², a white star, about 440. Light fades with the square of distance, so to look equally bright from more than twice as far, the orange star must give out roughly five times as much light.
card.answer: It is a match made only by perspective: a distant giant and a nearer white star that happen to line up.
card.wonder: The orange star’s light set out around the year 1050, about when Chinese astronomers recorded the supernova that left us the Crab Nebula.
card.connect: μ Boötis, nearby, is a pair that really does belong together.

stops.name: R Coronae Borealis
stops.plainClass: yellow supergiant, fades behind clouds of soot

getThere.text: From ν¹ & ν² Boötis, slide down and to the right about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (13°) to R Coronae Borealis, in Corona Borealis.

stops.whyHere: Most variable stars pulse, eclipse or explode; R Coronae Borealis has a stranger habit, disappearing now and then inside its own soot. It is tonight's challenge, so give it a patient minute and skip it without guilt if it stays hidden.
stops.transitionText: ν¹ & ν² Boötis is about 974 light-years away and R Coronae Borealis about 1,900–2,800 light-years, another long step outward.

card.question: How can a star vanish from view for months and then come back?
card.glance: At normal light, a 6th-magnitude star inside the Northern Crown's bowl; at other times, missing altogether.
card.see: Look inside the curve of Corona Borealis, about 2° north of δ CrB. At normal light R CrB is an easy binocular star, a little fainter than the Crown's faintest stars; if the spot is empty, the star is in a fade, and that is a real observation too.
card.understand: R CrB is a supergiant, a star swollen to enormous size, and an oddly built one, almost empty of hydrogen and rich in carbon. Now and then a puff of gas leaving its surface cools enough for that carbon to condense into soot, much as a candle flame blackens a cold spoon. When such a cloud forms on our side, the star sinks from 6th magnitude to as faint as 15th.
card.answer: It hides behind soot of its own making and stays hidden until the cloud drifts off and thins, which can take months or years. Its strange chemistry hints at an equally strange birth, perhaps two white dwarfs that merged into one swollen star.
card.wonder: At its deepest it is thousands of times fainter than normal, as if someone had drawn a curtain across a lamp.
card.connect: Three degrees away, T CrB waits to do the opposite: brighten without warning.

stops.name: Great Hercules Globular Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep left about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (14°) to the Great Hercules Globular Cluster, in Hercules.

stops.whyHere: With the Great Hercules Globular Cluster you reach deepest into the past. Most stars live in the Milky Way's flat disk, but its oldest families orbit in a vast halo around it, and M13 is the grandest of them in northern skies.
stops.transitionText: The Great Hercules Globular Cluster sits about 24,200 light-years away, about 10 times farther than R Coronae Borealis, so its light has a longer road behind it.

card.question: What does a city of half a million ancient stars look like from here?
card.glance: A small, round, soft glow on the west side of the Hercules Keystone, brighter toward its middle.
card.see: Find the four-star Keystone of Hercules. About a third of the way from η to ζ Herculis sits a fuzzy ball that is clearly not a star, brightening toward its center; beside a star of similar brightness, one is a point and the other a cloud.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight ball of stars born together when the Milky Way was young. M13 packs roughly half a million Suns' worth of them into about 120 light-years, a space that around the Sun holds only a few thousand stars. Its stars are poor in iron and the other heavy elements, so they must have formed before many generations of stars had lived and died.
card.answer: From here it is a soft, round glow, yet it holds about half a million stars some 12 billion years old. On a planet near its core, the night sky would be crowded with stars far brighter than any we see.
card.wonder: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message about humanity toward M13, and it will need roughly 24,000 years to arrive.
card.connect: M92, Hercules's second globular, looks smaller but is even older and poorer in heavy elements.

image.license: CC0
image.caption: Telescope photograph: thousands of resolved stars. Binoculars show only the soft central glow.

journeys.title: Partners or Strangers: The Doubles of Draco
journeys.drivingQuestion: How many stars can hide inside a single point of light?
journeys.hook: A single point of light can hold a whole family of stars circling one another.
journeys.story: Many stars that look single to the eye split into pairs in binoculars, and some pairs hold whole families. Count them from Polaris onward, and ask which pairs really belong together.
journeys.payoff: Alphecca looks like a single star to the eye, yet it holds a whole system, several stars sharing one point of light.
journeys.regionLabel: In the north-east, around Draco

stops.name: Polaris
stops.plainClass: yellow supergiant + yellow-white star, pulsating Cepheid

getThere.text: Find Polaris by eye, the Pole Star, at the end of the Little Dipper’s handle, about 40° up in the north; the two pointer stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl lead to it. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Count the stars of Polaris by eye, then count again in the binoculars, because the difference is tonight's whole subject.

card.question: How can the North Star help measure the distance to other galaxies?
card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole, sitting on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl up to Polaris, at the tip of the Little Dipper’s handle. Binoculars show it sitting on a little loop of fainter stars, the Engagement Ring, like the diamond on top. Its pulsing is far too slight for the eye to catch.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant, a big, bright aging star, and a Cepheid: it rhythmically swells and shrinks, here every four days, at a rate tied to its true brightness. The rule needs calibrating, and Polaris offers a rare chance. A close partner circles it about every 30 years, and an interferometer, which links telescopes to see fine detail, followed the orbit and weighed Polaris directly at about five Suns.
card.answer: Time a Cepheid’s beat and you know its true power; compare that with how faint it looks and you have its distance, and a nearby, weighable Cepheid like Polaris is where astronomers check that the rule is honest.
card.wonder: Close-up images from the CHARA telescope array show bright and dark patches on its surface that come and go.
card.connect: Polaris has not always been the pole star, and Kochab, nearby, once had the job.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, N. Evans (Harvard-Smithsonian CfA), and H. Bond (STScI)
image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: Hubble separates the North Star from its faint companion, Polaris B. A third star sits too close to Polaris to show here, so the North Star is really a triple.

stops.name: Psi Draconis

getThere.text: Move right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (18°), and Psi Draconis is there, in Draco.

stops.whyHere: Stars near the celestial pole never set, so a double there is a target for every season, and ψ Draconis is a neat one. The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: How bright a star looks depends on its distance too, and in truth Psi Draconis is about 370 times less luminous than Polaris.

card.question: Is there a binocular double that never sets?
card.glance: A 30″ pair of yellow-white stars high in Draco, circumpolar from mid-northern latitudes.
card.see: At 10× the pair splits cleanly, a brighter primary with a fainter companion just to the north. It sits high in Draco, not far from the Little Dipper.
card.understand: The two are Sun-like stars, slightly warmer than the Sun, about 74 light-years away. Because they lie so close to the pole, Earth's spin carries them around in a small circle instead of below the horizon. From mid-northern latitudes that circle never dips out of sight.
card.answer: ψ Draconis is one, a 30″ pair of Sun-like stars that circles the pole and never sets from mid-northern latitudes.
card.wonder: From a planet around either star, the other would hang in the sky as a brilliant point, bright enough to cast shadows.
card.connect: ν Draconis offers equal twins for comparison.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Close-up survey photograph of ψ Draconis.

stops.name: Nu Draconis

getThere.text: From Psi Draconis, slide right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (17°) to Nu Draconis, still in Draco.

stops.whyHere: After pairs that differ in color and brightness, ν Draconis is the opposite: two stars so alike they look like a reflection.
stops.transitionText: Underneath, Psi Draconis and Nu Draconis share one idea. Many stars are two or more; some are true orbiting pairs, others are chance alignments.

card.question: Can two stars really be perfect twins?
card.glance: Two perfectly matched white stars 62″ apart in the dragon's head: one of the finest binocular doubles.
card.see: Find the four-star head of Draco north-west of Vega, then its faintest star. Binoculars split it into two equal white points 62″ apart, like a pair of eyes looking back at you.
card.understand: The twins are white stars a little hotter than the Sun, about 98 light-years away, sharing a slow orbit around each other. Stars born from the same cloud at the same time with the same mass should live identical lives. Look closely at their light, though, and small differences appear.
card.answer: Very nearly, for the two look identical in binoculars, though their spectra show that one has a slightly unusual surface chemistry.
card.wonder: They are so evenly matched that it is hard to say which is brighter.
card.connect: ψ Draconis is a tighter, unequal pair.

stops.name: 16 & 17 Draconis

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (9°), and 16 & 17 Draconis is there, still in Draco.

stops.whyHere: Two stars side by side can be partners or strangers, and 16 and 17 Draconis make a gentle first case to puzzle over.
stops.transitionText: Nu Draconis and 16 & 17 Draconis shine, change or glow for the same underlying reason.

card.question: Is this easy pair in Draco really a family?
card.glance: A wide, nearly equal pair of white 5th-magnitude stars 90″ apart in Draco; easy in any binoculars.
card.see: Two matched white points sit 90″ apart, an easy split for any binoculars. A telescope would show that one of them is itself a 3″ pair.
card.understand: To decide whether stars belong together, astronomers check whether they share a distance and move across the sky in step. Gaia puts this system about 413 light-years away, and catalogs list a third star 3″ from one of the pair. Whether all three are truly bound by gravity is not yet settled.
card.answer: Probably, though it is not yet proven: the wide pair and the close third star look like a family, and only more precise motions will tell for sure.
card.wonder: Light from them left over 400 years ago, around the time Galileo first turned a telescope to the sky.
card.connect: Draco holds two more lovely binocular pairs, ν and ψ Draconis.

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (16°) to ν¹ & ν² Boötis, in Boötes.

stops.whyHere: ν Boötis looks like the best-matched pair in Boötes, two stars of equal brightness side by side.
stops.transitionText: Set side by side, 16 & 17 Draconis at about 3.8 times the Sun's radius and ν¹ & ν² Boötis at about 78–110 times the Sun's radius would look nothing alike.

card.glance: Two stars about a third of a Moon-width apart in northern Boötes, one orange and one white.
card.see: Start at Nekkar, the star at the top of the kite of Boötes, and sweep east. Binoculars show orange ν¹ and white ν² side by side, nearly equal in brightness.
card.understand: Gaia settles it by parallax, each star's tiny shift as Earth circles the Sun. Those shifts put ν¹, an orange giant, nearly 1,000 light-years away, and ν², a white star, about 440. Light fades with the square of distance, so to look equally bright from more than twice as far, the orange star must give out roughly five times as much light.
card.answer: It is a match made only by perspective: a distant giant and a nearer white star that happen to line up.
card.wonder: The orange star’s light set out around the year 1050, about when Chinese astronomers recorded the supernova that left us the Crab Nebula.
card.connect: μ Boötis, nearby, is a pair that really does belong together.

stops.name: Alphecca

getThere.text: Move right about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (14°), and Alphecca is there, in Corona Borealis.

stops.whyHere: Alphecca is the last point of light to count tonight. Alphecca anchors the hops to the Crown's two strange variables, and it hides a small surprise of its own.
stops.transitionText: Put each in the Sun's place and the difference would be enormous, because Alphecca is about 30 times smaller than ν¹ & ν² Boötis.

card.question: Is the Northern Crown's brightest jewel really a single star?
card.glance: The bright jewel of the Northern Crown, the small semicircle of stars between Arcturus and Vega.
card.see: Alphecca is the one bright star in the arc of Corona Borealis, and binoculars fit the whole crown into one or two fields. Start every hop to T CrB and R CrB here.
card.understand: Watched with sensitive instruments, its light dips slightly every 17 days. The dips come from two stars, a hot white one and a smaller Sun-like one, taking turns to pass in front of each other. We notice only because our line of sight lies almost in the plane of their orbit.
card.answer: Alphecca is an eclipsing pair whose dips are far too small for the eye, so its steady look hides a rhythm only instruments can catch.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 75 years ago, roughly a human lifetime.
card.connect: From this steady jewel, the crown's unpredictable stars are a short hop away.

journeys.title: The Restless Stars of Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: Aren't stars supposed to shine steadily?
journeys.hook: Stars look steady, yet some are pulsing, eclipsing or hiding behind their own dust.
journeys.story: The stars look as steady as streetlights, yet some swell and shrink, some are eclipsed by a partner, and some fade behind their own dust. Tonight you watch them as a variable-star observer would.
journeys.payoff: None of tonight's stars keeps still, and each changes for its own reason: swelling and shrinking, a partner passing in front, or dust drifting across its face.
journeys.difficultyReason: RW Cephei is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: Overhead, around Cepheus

stops.name: Garnet Star

getThere.text: Find Alderamin by eye, the brightest star of Cepheus, nearly overhead. From there, hop up about half a field of your 6.5° binoculars (5°) to the Garnet Star.

stops.whyHere: Not every star shines steadily, and the Garnet Star is the first tonight whose light rises and falls.

card.question: How big can a star grow, and why does the Garnet Star glow so red?
card.glance: A deep orange-red point at the edge of the Milky Way in Cepheus, one of the reddest stars you can see without optics.
card.see: Start at Alderamin, the brightest star of Cepheus, and look toward ζ Cephei; the Garnet Star sits a little south of the halfway point. In binoculars its color leaps out against the white stars around it, and a slightly soft focus deepens it toward the gem it is named for.
card.understand: Heat a poker and it glows red, then orange, then white, and stars follow the same rule. At about 3,700 K the Garnet Star’s surface is far cooler than the Sun’s, yet the star is visible from more than a thousand light-years away. A cool surface can only pour out that much light if it is enormous, and interferometers, which combine telescopes to measure its tiny disk, confirm it.
card.answer: It is a red supergiant, swollen to roughly a thousand times the Sun’s width near the end of its life, and its cool surface glows deep orange. Dust in front of it reddens it further, the way haze reddens a setting Sun.
card.wonder: Set it in the Sun’s place and its surface would lie far beyond the orbit of Mars, perhaps out toward Jupiter.
card.connect: A star this heavy will end as a supernova, scattering the elements it forged, as Betelgeuse in Orion will.

stops.name: VV Cephei
stops.plainClass: red supergiant + blue-white star, eclipsing binary

getThere.text: No hop needed: VV Cephei sits in the same view, below and to the right of the Garnet Star.

stops.whyHere: VV Cephei is a red supergiant with a hot blue partner, and the pair’s rare eclipses let astronomers size up a giant star by timing alone.
stops.transitionText: The Garnet Star and VV Cephei are red supergiants a few degrees apart, but only VV Cephei keeps a hot companion, which it passes in front of every 20 years.

card.question: How can an eclipse measure a star too distant to see as a disk?
card.glance: A modest orange star in Cepheus that shows no sign of being two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees north of the Garnet Star, so sweep between the two and compare them. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery, and its slow changes are too small to judge by eye.
card.understand: The star you see is a red supergiant, a heavyweight in the bloated last stage of its life, and a hot blue star circles it on an orbit we see nearly edge-on. Once every 20.3 years the giant swings in front of its partner and hides it for a long stretch. Knowing the blue star’s speed from its light, astronomers can treat the eclipse like a car passing behind a long wall: speed multiplied by time gives the length of the wall.
card.answer: The hidden star acts as a probe, and pacing out its passage behind the giant gives the giant’s width almost directly. Interferometers, which read its tiny disk, put it at hundreds of times the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: Its eclipses are among the longest known, the blue star staying hidden behind the giant for well over a year.
card.connect: Algol’s wink every few days and VV Cephei’s twenty-year eclipse are the same geometry, with only the size of the stars and their orbit changed.

stops.name: Caph

getThere.text: From VV Cephei, slide up and to the right about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (16°) to Caph, in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: Caph pulses every two and a half hours, far too gently for your eyes, so even a “steady” star can be breathing.
stops.transitionText: In the light they truly give off, VV Cephei shines with about 57,000–89,000 times the Sun's light and Caph with about 27 times the Sun's light.

card.question: Can a star that looks perfectly steady actually be pulsing?
card.glance: The western end of Cassiopeia’s W, a bright white star that looks steady to the eye.
card.see: Caph is the western end of the W of Cassiopeia, a clean white-yellow point. ρ Cassiopeiae lies about two and a half degrees west-south-west.
card.understand: Caph is a δ Scuti star, one of a family of pulsating stars a little hotter than the Sun. A layer near its surface works like the valve on a pressure cooker, trapping heat, swelling, venting and sinking back. Light meters catch the rhythm as a change of only a few hundredths of a magnitude.
card.answer: Caph does exactly that, swelling and shrinking about ten times a day, always too little for the eye, so its steadiness is only a limit of our senses.
card.wonder: One full pulse, out and back, takes about as long as a long film.
card.connect: ρ Cassiopeiae, a short hop away, varies far more and lies roughly 170 times farther off.

stops.name: RW Cephei

getThere.text: Move up about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°), and RW Cephei is there, in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: RW Cephei is one of the largest stars known in our galaxy, and it recently went through its own great dimming, much as Betelgeuse did.
stops.transitionText: Both look like points of light, yet RW Cephei is about 350 times larger than Caph.

card.question: Why did one of the largest stars in the galaxy suddenly fade?
card.glance: A modest orange star in southern Cepheus, easy in binoculars and unremarkable to look at.
card.see: RW Cephei lies about two and a half degrees south-south-west of δ Cephei, and binoculars show a modest orange point. Its brightness wanders over months, so note it against the stars around it.
card.understand: RW Cep is a hypergiant, an exceptionally heavy and luminous star swollen in a late, unstable stage. The CHARA array combines several telescopes into what acts like one giant instrument, and it shows a star between about 900 and 1,760 times wider than the Sun. During the recent fade one side looked darker than the other, which is not how a star that dims evenly would look.
card.answer: RW Cephei threw off gas that cooled into dust on one side, and the cloud blocked part of its light, much as a dusty veil dimmed Betelgeuse in 2019 and 2020. The star kept shining; a curtain had been drawn across our view.
card.wonder: The light reaching you left it about 11,000 years ago, around when people first began to farm.
card.connect: The Garnet Star, a few degrees away, is a red supergiant of the same size class, still shining unveiled.

stops.name: δ Cephei
stops.plainClass: yellow supergiant + blue-white star, pulsating Cepheid

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: δ Cephei is already in the same view, below and to the right of RW Cephei.

stops.whyHere: δ Cephei is the last of tonight's changing stars. It gave its name to the Cepheids, the pulsing stars whose beat became the first yardstick for distances beyond our galaxy.
stops.transitionText: Put each in the Sun's place and the difference would be enormous, because δ Cephei is about 30 times smaller than RW Cephei.

card.question: How did a star that pulses every five days become a ruler for the universe?
card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a blue-white companion beside it, brightening and fading on a strict five-day rhythm.
card.see: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house-shaped figure of Cepheus, with a fainter blue-white companion close beside it. Over several nights compare it with ζ Cephei, its match at peak, and ε Cephei, its match at the bottom, and you will see it brighten quickly and fade slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen late in life, and its outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt studied many such stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, all at nearly the same distance, so any difference in how bright they looked had to be real. The slower a star beat, she found, the brighter it truly was: time the pulse and you know its real power.
card.answer: Know a lamp’s true wattage, and how faint it looks tells you how far away it is. When Edwin Hubble caught the same beat in a star inside the Andromeda “nebula”, the universe grew enormously overnight.
card.wonder: Its cousins in distant galaxies still anchor the measurement of how fast the universe is expanding.
card.connect: β Cephei, elsewhere in the same constellation, pulses too, but every few hours and so gently that only instruments can tell.

journeys.title: Partners or Strangers: The Doubles of Cygnus
journeys.drivingQuestion: When you see one star, how many are really there?
journeys.hook: Many single-looking stars split in two in binoculars, and some pairs are real partners.
journeys.story: Many stars that look single to the eye split into pairs in binoculars, and some pairs hold whole families. Count them from the Double-Double onward, and ask which pairs really belong together.
journeys.payoff: 31 Cygni looks like a single star to the eye, yet it holds a whole system, several stars sharing one point of light.
journeys.difficultyReason: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the west, around Cygnus

stops.name: Double-Double
stops.plainClass: four white stars in two pairs

getThere.text: Find Vega by eye, the brilliant blue-white star of Lyra, brightest of the Summer Triangle, about 50° up in the west. From there, hop up about 2° (a fraction of one field of your 6.5° binoculars) to the Double-Double.

stops.whyHere: Many single-looking stars are really two or more, and the Double-Double is the first test of your counting.

card.question: How many stars can hide inside one faint point of light?
card.glance: Two matching white stars about 1.7° north-east of Vega in Lyra; any binoculars split them.
card.see: Put Vega at the edge of the field and look about 1.7° to the north-east: two matched white stars sit side by side like distant headlights. Very sharp eyes can see them as one slightly stretched star without optics, and any binoculars split them easily.
card.understand: Point a telescope at high power on either star and it splits again, into a pair a couple of arcseconds apart (an arcsecond is a 3,600th of a degree). Both close pairs lie at the same distance, about 158 light-years, and drift across the sky together, which would be a strange coincidence for strangers. Over centuries each pair circles its own balance point, and timing orbits like these is how astronomers weigh stars.
card.answer: Binoculars show two, a telescope shows four, and the shared distance and motion say all four form one family held together by gravity, so the dim point beside Vega is really a small stellar neighborhood.
card.wonder: The close pairs are about a hundred times tighter than the wide one, a system within a system.
card.connect: Two degrees south, Sheliak's two stars are packed so tightly they almost touch.

stops.name: Albireo

getThere.text: From the Double-Double, slide left about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (15°) to Albireo, in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Albireo is the sky's most beautiful color contrast, gold beside blue, and that contrast turns out to be a thermometer you can read from your backyard.
stops.transitionText: Albireo looks like a couple but is probably two siblings drifting apart, while the Double-Double is a genuine system of four.

card.question: Can you really read a star's temperature from its color?
card.glance: The swan's head in Cygnus, roughly halfway from Vega to Altair; steady binoculars split it into gold and blue.
card.see: Albireo marks the head of the swan, at the foot of the Northern Cross. Brace your binoculars on something solid and at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white spark beside it, 34″ away; if the split is hard, let the image drift and watch for the blue point trailing behind.
card.understand: Think of an electric stove ring as it heats: first dull red, then orange, and, if it could get hot enough, white and then blue. Stars are glowing balls of gas and follow the same rule. Their spectra pin down the numbers: the gold star is a cool giant near 4,400 K, the blue one about 13,000 K.
card.answer: You can, and Albireo proves it: the golden star is only about a third as hot as its blue companion, and your eye registers that gap as color. Every tint you notice tonight is a surface temperature read across hundreds of light-years.
card.wonder: For a century Albireo was the textbook orbiting pair; precise Gaia-era motions now suggest two siblings born together and slowly drifting apart.
card.connect: The Double-Double near Vega shows pairs that truly do orbit each other.

stops.name: Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868)

getThere.text: Sweep up about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (9°) to Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868), still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Most heavy stars end their lives out of sight, but here in the swan's neck is one of the first places where astronomers became sure black holes are real. It is tonight's challenge, so give it a patient minute and skip it without guilt if it stays hidden.
stops.transitionText: Rank them by real output rather than by eye and Albireo gives about 1,560 times the Sun's light while Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) gives about 360,000–500,000 times the Sun's light.

card.question: Can you see a star that is orbiting a black hole?
card.glance: A 9th-magnitude star half a degree from η Cygni in the swan's neck: unremarkable, unforgettable once you know.
card.see: Center η Cygni, midway along the swan's neck. About 0.4° to the east-north-east, less than a Moon's width away, a 9th-magnitude star slightly brighter than its neighbors is HDE 226868, and nothing about it looks special.
card.understand: This blue supergiant, about 40 times the Sun's mass, whips around an unseen partner every 5.6 days. Weighing the partner uses the same trick as weighing planets: measure how fast and how far the visible star swings to and fro, and gravity tells you what must be pulling it. In 2021 radio measurements pinned down the distance, and the partner came out at about 21 Suns while giving off no starlight at all.
card.answer: You are looking at one. An object that heavy which gives off no light of its own can only be a black hole, the collapsed core of a massive star, and gas torn from the supergiant glows in X-rays as it spirals in.
card.wonder: The light you see set off over seven thousand years ago, before writing was invented.
card.connect: The Veil Nebula shows the other way a heavy star can end: blown apart.

stops.name: 16 Cygni B

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (16°), and 16 Cygni B is there, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: Planet hunting began with stars like the Sun, and 16 Cygni is the summer sky's best test: two Sun-like stars born together, only one with a known giant planet.
stops.transitionText: In the light they truly give off, Cygnus X-1 (HDE 226868) shines with about 360,000–500,000 times the Sun's light and 16 Cygni B with about 1.3 times the Sun's light.

card.question: What would our Sun be like with a twin beside it?
card.glance: One of a matched pair of 6th-magnitude yellowish stars 40″ apart, on the swan's western wing in Cygnus.
card.see: From δ Cygni, go about 5° north with the chart to a pair of equal faint stars 40″ apart, split at 10× on a steady mount. Both share a soft yellow-white tint, and 16 Cyg B is the slightly fainter one, to the south-east.
card.understand: Both stars are close copies of the Sun in temperature and mass. Stars ring like bells, and since the tones depend on what is inside, the Kepler spacecraft's measurements of their tiny pulsations gave both an age of about 6.8 billion years, older than the Sun. In 1996 astronomers found a planet at least 1.5 times Jupiter's mass circling B once every 2.2 years on a strongly stretched orbit.
card.answer: It would look much like 16 Cygni, two near-identical suns sharing a long, wide orbit and tugging on each other's planets. B's giant may owe its wildly stretched path to its sibling, a hint that our own calm, round orbits are a privilege of a single star.
card.wonder: From that planet, 16 Cygni A would shine as a brilliant second sun.
card.connect: HD 189733, near the Dumbbell Nebula, has a planet whose color has been measured.

stops.name: 31 Cygni

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the left about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°) to 31 Cygni, still in Cygnus.

stops.whyHere: The night's counting ends at 31 Cygni, an orange supergiant. Albireo's gold-and-blue lesson can be hard to split, and 31 Cygni repeats it with room to spare, plus a secret of its own.
stops.transitionText: 31 Cygni is about 3,800 times more luminous than 16 Cygni B, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.question: Can binoculars show Albireo's colors with an easier split?
card.glance: An orange star 5° west-north-west of Deneb with a blue-white companion: a binocular color group with 30 Cygni.
card.see: Binoculars show orange 31 Cyg with white 30 Cyg about 5½′ away and a fainter star closer in. The gaps are wider than Albireo's, so the colors come easily.
card.understand: 31 Cygni is an orange supergiant, a cool star swollen to huge size. A hot blue star orbits it and slips behind it every 10.4 years. As the blue star sinks, its light shines for a while through the giant's thin outer atmosphere, so astronomers can probe that air like a lamp seen through fog.
card.answer: 31 Cygni does, pairing an orange supergiant with blue-white neighbors set wide enough for any binoculars.
card.wonder: The orange star is about 160 times wider than the Sun, so its companion takes weeks to creep behind it.
card.connect: Albireo shows the same colors at a tighter split.

journeys.title: Look-Alikes of Cassiopeia
journeys.drivingQuestion: What hidden difference sets look-alike stars apart?
journeys.hook: Two stars can look alike and live opposite lives; tonight you find what parts them.
journeys.story: The sky looks flat, so stars that seem like neighbors or twins can be anything but. Tonight is a game of spot-the-difference, played with real physics.
journeys.payoff: What your eye sees, color and brightness, is only the surface; underneath, each look-alike pair differed in temperature, age, distance or mass, and that difference shaped their lives.
journeys.difficultyReason: η Cassiopeiae is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the west, around Cassiopeia

stops.name: γ Cassiopeiae
stops.plainClass: blue-white star, fast spinner with a gas disk

getThere.text: Find γ Cassiopeiae by eye, the middle star of the W of Cassiopeia, about 55° up in the north-west. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Tonight's stars look alike at first and lead very different lives, so take in the color and brightness of γ Cassiopeiae, because both can mislead.

card.question: Why has the middle star of Cassiopeia’s W brightened and faded over the decades?
card.glance: The blue-white center star of Cassiopeia’s W, plain to look at but wrapped in a disk of glowing gas.
card.see: γ Cas is the middle star of the W, a clean blue-white point in binoculars. Swing to orange Schedar, the next bright star west, and back: over the decades γ has sometimes outshone Schedar and sometimes fallen below it, so your comparison tonight joins a long record.
card.understand: γ Cas is about 8 million years old, many times heavier than the Sun, and spinning so fast that its equator barely holds on. Gas leaks off that bulging equator into a flattened disk, like mud flung from a spinning wheel. In 1866 Angelo Secchi spread its light into a spectrum and saw bright lines where dark ones belong, a first for any star, and those lines come from the glowing disk.
card.answer: The star stays much the same while its disk comes and goes, adding its glow as it builds and taking it away as it thins. That is why the W’s middle star has wandered between about magnitudes 1.6 and 3.0.
card.wonder: Its light set out in the late Middle Ages, so tonight you see the disk it wore more than five centuries ago.
card.connect: Spin shapes stars: Alderamin in Cepheus is flattened by its spin, and γ Cas spins hard enough to shed a disk.

stops.name: η Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: Stay put: η Cassiopeiae is in the same view, below and to the left of γ Cassiopeiae.

stops.whyHere: η Cassiopeiae is a near-twin of the Sun only 19 light-years away, which makes it a mirror held up to our own star. The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: η Cas and γ Cas sit side by side in the W, but γ Cas is nearly thirty times farther away, so the W is a trick of perspective.

card.question: What would our Sun look like from a neighboring star?
card.glance: A pale yellow star in Cassiopeia’s W with a faint orange companion that steady, high-power binoculars can sometimes split.
card.see: η Cas sits between Schedar and γ Cas in the W. Its companion is only 13 arcseconds away and far fainter, so most hand-held binoculars show a single star. Brace 10× or larger binoculars on something solid and look for a tiny orange dot pressed against the yellow glare.
card.understand: The bright star is close to a twin of the Sun, slightly hotter, and its companion is a cooler, smaller orange dwarf. Observers have recorded the pair since 1779, and over those centuries the companion has swung a long way around its orbit. Kepler’s laws turn the size and period of an orbit into the mass that drives it, so this slow dance weighs both stars.
card.answer: Move the Sun out to 19 light-years and it would shine at about the brightness of η Cassiopeiae itself, a modest naked-eye star. Somewhere out there, an observer could be looking at our Sun as just another point in their sky.
card.wonder: Seen from η Cassiopeiae, our Sun would sit in the opposite part of the sky, close to the stars we call the Southern Cross.
card.connect: γ Cas, right beside it in the W and brighter to the eye, is nearly thirty times farther away.

stops.name: Schedar

getThere.text: No hop needed: Schedar sits in the same view, just below η Cassiopeiae.

stops.whyHere: Schedar is an aging orange giant, an easy color contrast to the hot blue-white stars in the middle of the W.
stops.transitionText: Schedar is about 650 times more luminous than η Cassiopeiae, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.question: Why is Schedar orange when its neighbors in the W are white?
card.glance: An orange star in Cassiopeia, warmer in tint than its white neighbors in the W.
card.see: Schedar is the bright southern point of Cassiopeia’s W. Swing to γ Cas at the center of the W and back to compare colors.
card.understand: A star’s color is set by its surface temperature, just as a stove ring glows red before it glows white. Schedar has used up the hydrogen in its core, and as the core contracted, the outer layers swelled. Spread over a much larger surface, the heat escapes from a cooler skin.
card.answer: Schedar is an aging giant whose swollen surface has cooled to orange. Orange here means cooler than the Sun, not weaker: it still gives off hundreds of times the Sun’s light.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 230 years ago, before anyone had measured the distance to any star.
card.connect: Hot blue-white γ Cas, the next bright star east, makes the color contrast plain.

card.see: Caph is the western end of the W of Cassiopeia, a clean white-yellow point. ρ Cassiopeiae lies about two and a half degrees west-south-west.
card.understand: Caph is a δ Scuti star, one of a family of pulsating stars a little hotter than the Sun. A layer near its surface works like the valve on a pressure cooker, trapping heat, swelling, venting and sinking back. Light meters catch the rhythm as a change of only a few hundredths of a magnitude.
card.answer: Caph does exactly that, swelling and shrinking about ten times a day, always too little for the eye, so its steadiness is only a limit of our senses.

stops.name: ρ Cassiopeiae

getThere.text: No hop needed: ρ Cassiopeiae sits in the same view, just below Caph.

stops.whyHere: With ρ Cassiopeiae, a yellow hypergiant, the night's last pair of look-alikes is complete. It is a yellow hypergiant, a star at the very top of the power scale, and a lesson in how badly faintness can mislead.
stops.transitionText: ρ Cassiopeiae shares this patch of sky with Caph, yet it is about 170 times farther, a trick of perspective.

card.question: How can a star you can barely see be one of the sky’s most powerful?
card.glance: A faint yellowish star near Caph in Cassiopeia that looks entirely ordinary.
card.see: Start at Caph, the western end of Cassiopeia’s W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to a faint yellowish star. σ Cassiopeiae lies just south, with the soft glow of NGC 7789 between them.
card.understand: Most stars that look bright are simply close, and ρ Cas is the opposite case. Astronomers fix its distance from the family of stars it travels with and measure its true width with interferometers, and together those give its real output. A star this extreme, roughly 40 times the Sun’s mass, lives in a brief, unstable late stage, and in 2000 it dimmed, cooled sharply and threw off a shell of gas.
card.answer: From about 9,000 light-years away, a star needs more than half a million times the Sun’s output to reach your eye at all, and ρ Cassiopeiae has it. The faint dot near Caph is one of the most luminous stars you can see.
card.wonder: That single outburst in 2000 shed gas weighing roughly 10,000 Earths.
card.connect: Power, not closeness, puts it in your sky: η Cassiopeiae, brighter to the eye, is only about 19 light-years away.

journeys.title: Partners or Strangers: The Doubles of Cepheus
journeys.drivingQuestion: How many stars can hide inside a single point of light?
journeys.hook: A single point of light can hold a whole family of stars circling one another.
journeys.story: Your eye sees one point of light, binoculars sometimes see two, and physics often finds more. From δ Cephei to Polaris, tonight is an exercise in counting stars that hide behind one another.
journeys.payoff: Some pairs are true partners and some only line up by chance, and Polaris is the real thing, stars held together by gravity and circling one another.
journeys.difficultyReason: U Cephei is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Cepheus

stops.name: δ Cephei
stops.plainClass: yellow supergiant + blue-white star, pulsating Cepheid

getThere.text: Find Alderamin by eye, the brightest star of Cepheus, about 35° up in the north-west. From there, hop up and to the left about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (10°) to δ Cephei.

stops.whyHere: Many single-looking stars are really two or more, and δ Cephei is the first test of your counting.

card.question: How did a star that pulses every five days become a ruler for the universe?
card.glance: A yellowish star in Cepheus with a blue-white companion beside it, brightening and fading on a strict five-day rhythm.
card.see: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house-shaped figure of Cepheus, with a fainter blue-white companion close beside it. Over several nights compare it with ζ Cephei, its match at peak, and ε Cephei, its match at the bottom, and you will see it brighten quickly and fade slowly.
card.understand: δ Cephei is a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen late in life, and its outer layers rise and fall every 5.37 days. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt studied many such stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, all at nearly the same distance, so any difference in how bright they looked had to be real. The slower a star beat, she found, the brighter it truly was: time the pulse and you know its real power.
card.answer: Know a lamp’s true wattage, and how faint it looks tells you how far away it is. When Edwin Hubble caught the same beat in a star inside the Andromeda “nebula”, the universe grew enormously overnight.
card.wonder: Its cousins in distant galaxies still anchor the measurement of how fast the universe is expanding.
card.connect: β Cephei, elsewhere in the same constellation, pulses too, but every few hours and so gently that only instruments can tell.

stops.name: VV Cephei
stops.plainClass: red supergiant + blue-white star, eclipsing binary

getThere.text: Sweep right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (7°) to VV Cephei, still in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: VV Cephei is a red supergiant with a hot blue partner, and the pair’s rare eclipses let astronomers size up a giant star by timing alone.
stops.transitionText: VV Cephei is about 40 times more luminous than δ Cephei, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.question: How can an eclipse measure a star too distant to see as a disk?
card.glance: A modest orange star in Cepheus that shows no sign of being two stars, one of them enormous.
card.see: VV Cephei lies a few degrees north of the Garnet Star, so sweep between the two and compare them. Both look orange, but VV is fainter and less fiery, and its slow changes are too small to judge by eye.
card.understand: The star you see is a red supergiant, a heavyweight in the bloated last stage of its life, and a hot blue star circles it on an orbit we see nearly edge-on. Once every 20.3 years the giant swings in front of its partner and hides it for a long stretch. Knowing the blue star’s speed from its light, astronomers can treat the eclipse like a car passing behind a long wall: speed multiplied by time gives the length of the wall.
card.answer: The hidden star acts as a probe, and pacing out its passage behind the giant gives the giant’s width almost directly. Interferometers, which read its tiny disk, put it at hundreds of times the Sun’s width.
card.wonder: Its eclipses are among the longest known, the blue star staying hidden behind the giant for well over a year.
card.connect: Algol’s wink every few days and VV Cephei’s twenty-year eclipse are the same geometry, with only the size of the stars and their orbit changed.

stops.name: Errai

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (16°), and Errai is there, still in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: Errai is where astronomers first glimpsed a planet’s signal, in 1988, years before anyone was ready to believe in planets around other suns.
stops.transitionText: How bright a star looks depends on its distance too, and in truth Errai is about 6,300 times less luminous than VV Cephei.

card.question: Why did the first hint of a planet around another star take fifteen years to accept?
card.glance: A pale orange star at the top of the house of Cepheus, the corner nearest Polaris.
card.see: Errai is the apex of the house of Cepheus, pointing toward Polaris, and binoculars show it as a pale orange point. Neither its small red companion nor its planet can be seen. Compare its warm tint with white Alderamin at the lower corner of the house.
card.understand: Errai is a little heavier than the Sun and has finished burning its core hydrogen, so it is starting to swell into a giant. In 1988 a Canadian team noticed a slow, repeating wobble in its speed, the tug a planet would produce. But the surface of a swelling star can pulse, spot and churn, and any of those can fake a wobble.
card.answer: Only years of further measurements could show that the signal kept perfect time like an orbit, and in 2003 a planet on a roughly two-and-a-half-year orbit was confirmed. By then 51 Pegasi had made such planets believable.
card.wonder: Its planet, at least one and a half times Jupiter’s mass, circles a star that has a faint red-dwarf partner, so it is a world in a double-star system.
card.connect: In 1995 the planet of 51 Pegasi ended the doubt that Errai’s signal had started.

stops.name: U Cephei

getThere.text: Move up and to the right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°), and U Cephei is there, still in Cepheus.

stops.whyHere: U Cephei plays Algol’s trick far more deeply, and binoculars let you follow the whole performance from a garden chair. It is tonight's challenge, so give it a patient minute and skip it without guilt if it stays hidden.
stops.transitionText: Errai and U Cephei look like neighbors, but U Cephei is about 10 times farther.

card.question: How can a star almost vanish and return in a single evening?
card.glance: A faint star near the north celestial pole that, every two and a half days, nearly disappears from binoculars for a few hours.
card.see: U Cephei lies about seven degrees from Polaris toward Cassiopeia’s W; find it with a chart and check the app’s predicted eclipse. Outside eclipse it is an easy binocular star, but near mid-eclipse it sinks to the limit of 50 mm binoculars, and the fade and recovery happen while you watch.
card.understand: U Cep is an eclipsing binary, two stars taking turns hiding each other: a hot blue-white star and a larger, cooler yellow one. The bigger the front star compared with the one behind, and the more squarely it crosses, the deeper the dip, and here the cool star is wide enough to cover its partner almost completely. As in Algol, the cool star has already swollen and spills gas onto its hot partner.
card.answer: Every 2.49 days the cool star passes almost squarely in front of the hot one, which does most of the shining, so the light drops to about a tenth. Algol only falls to a third; U Cephei comes close to switching off.
card.wonder: You can watch a star nearly disappear and return in the time it takes to have dinner and a long conversation.
card.connect: RZ Cassiopeiae, not far away, plays the same trick faster but more shallowly.

stops.name: Polaris
stops.plainClass: yellow supergiant + yellow-white star, pulsating Cepheid

getThere.text: Move right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (7°), and Polaris is there, in Ursa Minor.

stops.whyHere: The night's counting ends at Polaris, a yellow supergiant. It is more than the pivot of the northern sky; it is also the nearest of a special breed of pulsing star.
stops.transitionText: In the light they truly give off, U Cephei shines with about 65 times the Sun's light and Polaris with about 2,210 times the Sun's light.

card.question: How can the North Star help measure the distance to other galaxies?
card.glance: A steady, pale yellow star almost exactly at the pole, sitting on the edge of a small ring of fainter stars.
card.see: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper’s bowl up to Polaris, at the tip of the Little Dipper’s handle. Binoculars show it sitting on a little loop of fainter stars, the Engagement Ring, like the diamond on top. Its pulsing is far too slight for the eye to catch.
card.understand: Polaris is a yellow supergiant, a big, bright aging star, and a Cepheid: it rhythmically swells and shrinks, here every four days, at a rate tied to its true brightness. The rule needs calibrating, and Polaris offers a rare chance. A close partner circles it about every 30 years, and an interferometer, which links telescopes to see fine detail, followed the orbit and weighed Polaris directly at about five Suns.
card.answer: Time a Cepheid’s beat and you know its true power; compare that with how faint it looks and you have its distance, and a nearby, weighable Cepheid like Polaris is where astronomers check that the rule is honest.
card.wonder: Close-up images from the CHARA telescope array show bright and dark patches on its surface that come and go.
card.connect: Polaris has not always been the pole star, and Kochab, nearby, once had the job.

journeys.title: Cloud, Star, Cinder: A Life Told in Auriga
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where do stars come from, and how do they end?
journeys.hook: One patch of sky holds every chapter of a star's life, from cold cloud to cinders.
journeys.story: Nothing in a star's life is wasted. The gas a dying star returns to space becomes the next generation, and tonight's stops follow that cycle from start to finish.
journeys.payoff: Stars condense out of cold clouds, shine on the fuel in their cores, and finally hand their gas back to space, where it builds new stars and planets, ours among them.
journeys.difficultyReason: M37 is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Auriga

stops.name: Christmas Tree Cluster
stops.plainClass: newborn cluster still inside its cloud

getThere.text: Find Betelgeuse by eye, the orange-red shoulder star of Orion, about 45° up in the south-east. From there, hop left about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (12°) to the Christmas Tree Cluster.

stops.whyHere: A star's life begins in cold gas, so that is where we start: the Christmas Tree Cluster is a nursery where new stars are still taking shape.

card.question: What is the Christmas Tree Cluster still doing in its cloud?
card.glance: A bright star at the base of a small triangle of fainter stars, like an upside-down Christmas tree.
card.see: Go a little under halfway from Betelgeuse to Procyon, then about three and a half degrees north into Monoceros. The bright star S Monocerotis marks the trunk, and a narrow triangle of fainter stars points south to the tip, so the tree hangs upside down.
card.understand: Its stars formed between one and five million years ago, and they range from less than a tenth of the Sun’s mass to several times more. S Monocerotis, the bright trunk star, is far hotter and heavier than the Sun, and its light eats into the surrounding gas. X-ray telescopes pick out the youngest stars, which flare far more violently than adult stars, so astronomers can count the family even where dust hides it.
card.answer: It is still making stars: at the tree’s tip the Cone Nebula is a dark pillar of gas collapsing into new ones, even as the older siblings below erode it.
card.wonder: The Cone’s dust pillar alone is about seven light-years long.
card.connect: A few degrees south, the Rosette holds a bigger family of about the same age.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of NGC 2264: the bright star S Mon and the triangle of the “tree”.

stops.name: M35

getThere.text: From the Christmas Tree Cluster, slide up about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (16°) to M35, in Gemini.

stops.whyHere: M35 is a big young family close in age to the Pleiades, with a surprise hiding at its edge.
stops.transitionText: Blow away the birth cloud around stars like those of the Christmas Tree Cluster and you are left with something like M35, a young family in the open.

card.question: Why does M35 look fainter than the Pleiades though they are the same age?
card.glance: A rich, glittering patch near Gemini’s feet, with many stars resolved and visible to the eye on a dark night.
card.see: Find Gemini’s feet, η and μ Geminorum, and move about two degrees north-west. M35 is a round, grainy glow sprinkled with resolved stars, about the size of the full Moon, and just south-west lies a much smaller smudge, NGC 2158.
card.understand: M35’s age was found in an unusual way. Young stars spin fast and slowly brake as they age, like a top winding down, so the rotation periods of hundreds of its Sun-like stars make a clock, and it reads about 150 million years, close to the Pleiades. Gaia counts about 1,600 members.
card.answer: It is a matter of distance, for at about six times the Pleiades’ distance only M35’s brightest stars show individually and the rest merge into a glow.
card.wonder: The spin clock agrees with the other methods, which is why astronomers trust it for lone stars like the Sun.
card.connect: The little smudge at its edge, NGC 2158, is not part of this family at all.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of M35 with the compact NGC 2158 at its south-west edge.

stops.name: M37

getThere.text: Sweep up about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (9°) to M37, in Auriga.

stops.whyHere: M37 is the oldest and richest of the Auriga trio, half a billion years of cluster aging in a single view. It is tonight's challenge, so give it a patient minute and skip it without guilt if it stays hidden.
stops.transitionText: From a family the age of the Pleiades you move to one about three times older, just across the Auriga border.

card.question: What does half a billion years do to a star cluster?
card.glance: A round, rich, granular glow on the Auriga–Taurus border, where few stars break through.
card.see: From M36 in Auriga move about four degrees south-east, toward Gemini. M37 looks like a ball of fine sugar, rich and even, with only a handful of points resolved.
card.understand: M37 is more than twenty times older than M36, and its brightest members are now orange giants, stars that swelled after using up the fuel in their cores. Astronomers dated it two independent ways: from the point where its stars begin to swell, and from how far its white dwarfs, the cooling cores of stars already dead, have cooled. The two clocks agree on about 500 million years.
card.answer: It takes the heavy blue stars first and then the next heaviest, leaving thousands of modest stars of similar brightness that blend into a grainy glow beneath a few orange giants.
card.wonder: Gaia counts more than 2,400 members, the most of any cluster in Auriga’s trio.
card.connect: Three families, three ages, at broadly similar distances: together they make the sky’s best cluster clock.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of M37: a dense, even swarm of faint stars.

stops.name: Capella

getThere.text: Sweep up about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (15°) to Capella, still in Auriga.

stops.whyHere: Capella looks like one golden star, yet it is two giants in a tight embrace, and the way they were weighed is a small masterpiece.
stops.transitionText: Capella is where a star from a family like M37 is headed, the giant stage.

card.question: How can two giant stars hide inside a single point of light?
card.glance: The golden leader of Auriga, riding high on winter evenings.
card.see: Capella is the brilliant yellowish star high overhead on winter evenings, leading the pentagon of Auriga. Its creamy, slightly golden tint sits halfway between Rigel’s ice and Aldebaran’s orange. Just south of it lies the thin triangle of fainter stars called the Kids.
card.understand: The two stars circle each other every 104 days, so close that only interferometers, which combine several telescopes into one sharp eye, can separate them. Follow the orbit and the same laws that weigh the planets give the masses: about two and a half Suns each. Add each star’s measured size and temperature and something odd appears, because one already burns helium in its core, the fuel of a star’s later years, while its near-twin is only now swelling into a giant.
card.answer: Each giant is about ten times wider than the Sun, yet from 43 light-years their whole orbit shrinks to a speck that only an interferometer can open up.
card.wonder: A difference of a few percent in mass was enough to put two stars born together in different chapters of life.
card.connect: Next door in the Kids, a stranger pair hides one star inside a vast dark disk.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the Capella field.

stops.name: ε Aurigae

getThere.text: No hop needed: ε Aurigae sits in the same view, just right of Capella.

stops.whyHere: ε Aurigae, a white supergiant, carries the life story to its latest stage tonight. Every 27 years something huge and dark slides in front of ε Aurigae, and it took astronomers nearly two centuries to get a look at it.
stops.transitionText: Just south of Capella, whose two giants were weighed by their orbit, lies ε Aurigae, a pair whose second member hides inside a dark disk.

card.question: What could block a star’s light for almost two years?
card.glance: A modest star at the top of the Kids, the small triangle just south of Capella in Auriga.
card.see: From Capella, drop a few degrees south to the thin triangle of the Kids; ε Aurigae is the brightest of the three. Between eclipses it looks unremarkable, a steady white point. Its neighbor ζ Aurigae, the western star of the lower pair, has eclipses of its own every two and a half years.
card.understand: ε Aurigae is an eclipsing binary, a pair whose orbit, seen edge-on, carries one member in front of the other. The puzzle was the eclipse itself: it lasts almost two years, so whatever passes in front must be enormous, yet it gives off almost no light of its own. During the 2009 to 2011 eclipse, interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, finally caught the culprit in silhouette.
card.answer: It is a vast, dark, tilted disk of dust, many times wider than Earth’s orbit and probably hiding a smaller star inside, that slides across the bright star once every 27 years.
card.wonder: The next eclipse should begin around 2036–37, so there is still time to get to know the star before it happens.
card.connect: Its neighbor in the Kids hides a different eclipse, one you wait out in weeks rather than decades.

journeys.title: Perseus, Rung by Rung
journeys.drivingQuestion: How far away is the most distant thing you can see tonight?
journeys.hook: Start with a star next door and climb outward, each rung farther than the last.
journeys.story: Brightness is a poor guide to distance, since a modest star nearby can outshine a giant far away. Tonight you climb outward from Algol, each stop farther than the last.
journeys.payoff: Algol was the nearest and the Andromeda Galaxy the farthest, its light taking about 2.5 million years to reach you. Brightness alone would never have told you that order, but measurement did.
journeys.difficultyReason: Trumpler 2 is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Perseus

stops.name: Algol
stops.plainClass: blue-white star + orange star, eclipsing binary

getThere.text: Find Algol by eye, the Demon Star of Perseus, about 70° up in the south-west. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: To measure the depth of the sky you start close to home, and Algol is the first rung, near enough that its light takes about 90 years to reach you.

card.question: Why does Algol, the Demon Star, lose two-thirds of its light every few days?
card.glance: A white star in Perseus that looks perfectly ordinary until, every few days, it slips to a third of its usual brightness for a few hours.
card.see: Algol sits in Perseus, about halfway between Cassiopeia’s W and the Pleiades, and your eyes alone can follow it. At full light it matches Almach, the golden star at the end of Andromeda; deep in eclipse it sinks to the level of ε Persei.
card.understand: Algol is a close pair of stars, with a third circling farther out, and we see the pair’s orbit almost edge-on: an eclipsing binary. Every 2.87 days the dim orange companion slides across the hot blue-white star. The shape of the change gives it away: a pulsing star brightens and fades all the time, while Algol holds steady for most of its cycle and then drops sharply for a few hours, just as a passing body would make it.
card.answer: Neither star changes; the fainter one simply passes in front of the brighter and blocks most of its light until it moves on. The Demon’s wink is a shadow play, staged nearly 90 light-years away.
card.wonder: The companion is the lighter star yet the more aged one, because it swelled first and poured much of its gas onto its partner, turning the former heavyweight into the lightweight.
card.connect: Mira and δ Cephei change for the opposite reason: the star itself swells and shrinks.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the 3.7° field around Algol; bright stars appear as saturated disks, so sizes in the photo are not real sizes.

stops.name: Mirfak

getThere.text: From Algol, slide up and to the right about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (9°) to Mirfak, still in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: Mirfak is the brightest member of the Alpha Persei Cluster, a young star family that fits in one binocular view and shows two stages of life at once.
stops.transitionText: Mirfak sits about 506 light-years away, about 6 times farther than Algol, so its light has a longer road behind it.

card.question: Why is Mirfak yellower than the blue-white stars that surround it?
card.glance: The brightest star of Perseus, yellow-white and ringed in binoculars by a swarm of blue-white stars.
card.see: Aim at Mirfak, between Capella and Cassiopeia’s W, and the field fills with dozens of blue-white stars strung in curving chains, with Mirfak a shade yellower than the rest. Wide, low-power binoculars frame this cluster better than any telescope.
card.understand: An open cluster is a family of stars born together from one gas cloud, so its members share a birthday and a distance. That makes it a natural experiment in which the one big difference is how much mass each star started with. Heavy stars burn their fuel disproportionately fast, so the heaviest runs out of core hydrogen first and swells while its lighter siblings carry on.
card.answer: Mirfak started out the heaviest of the family, about seven times the Sun’s mass, so it has already swollen into a yellow supergiant while its siblings still shine blue-white. It managed all that in about 41 million years, a blink beside the Sun’s billions.
card.wonder: Mirfak and its siblings still travel through space together, a family that has stayed close for tens of millions of years.
card.connect: In the older Pleiades, stars as heavy as Mirfak have already burned out.
