stops.name: Trumpler 2

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (9°) to Trumpler 2, still in Perseus.

stops.whyHere: Trumpler 2 is a small, nearby family that sits on the sky close to the far-off Double Cluster. It is tonight's challenge, so give it a patient minute and skip it without guilt if it stays hidden.
stops.transitionText: From Mirfak at about 506 light-years the view reaches out to Trumpler 2 at about 2,200 light-years, about 4 times farther.

card.question: How far away is the little group east of the Double Cluster?
card.glance: A loose group of a dozen stars about two degrees west of Miram, east of the Double Cluster.
card.see: Center Miram, η Persei, and look about two degrees west. Pick out the brighter stars first, then let the fainter scatter fill in around them.
card.understand: Trumpler 2 is roughly 90 million years old. Gaia picks out about 450 members by their shared motion and averages their parallaxes into one distance. That distance turns out to be far smaller than the Double Cluster’s.
card.answer: About 2,200 light-years, less than a third as far as the Double Cluster, which only looks like its neighbor. One sweep of the binoculars spans thousands of light-years of depth.
card.wonder: When this family was born, dinosaurs still ruled the Earth.
card.connect: Swing west to the Double Cluster to compare a near family with a far one.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of Tr 2.

stops.name: Owl Cluster (ET Cluster)

getThere.text: From Trumpler 2, slide down about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (11°) to the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), in Cassiopeia.

stops.whyHere: The Owl Cluster is a young family with an open puzzle: is its brightest eye a member, or a star in front?
stops.transitionText: Trumpler 2 is about 2,200 light-years away and the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster) about 9,130 light-years, another long step outward.

card.question: Does the Owl Cluster’s bright eye really belong to the cluster?
card.glance: Two bright “eyes” at one end of a small, elongated swarm in Cassiopeia, like an owl or the movie alien ET.
card.see: Two degrees south of Ruchbah, find a pair of stars, one much brighter than the other; the bright one is φ Cassiopeiae. A faint, slightly elongated spray trails away from them, and steady binoculars turn it into outstretched wings or arms.
card.understand: The cluster is about 9,000 light-years away and only some 20 million years old. If φ Cassiopeiae belongs to it, it must be a yellow supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life; if it lies in front, it is just an ordinary bright star. Gaia’s parallax for φ Cas matches the cluster’s, but very bright stars are hard for Gaia to measure, and its speed toward us differs somewhat from older values.
card.answer: Probably, since the evidence leans toward membership, which would make the owl’s eye one of the most luminous stars in our galaxy. The case is not closed, and that is part of the fun.
card.wonder: If φ Cas is a member, the light reaching you set out about 9,000 years ago.
card.connect: M103, a degree from Ruchbah, is a cluster whose stars clearly belong together.

stops.name: Andromeda Galaxy

getThere.text: From the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster), slide down and to the left about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (18°) to the Andromeda Galaxy, in Andromeda.

stops.whyHere: The ladder ends at the Andromeda Galaxy, a spiral galaxy. It is a whole other galaxy, and for most people the most distant thing they will ever see unaided.
stops.transitionText: The Andromeda Galaxy lies about 2,480,000 light-years away, about 270 times farther than the Owl Cluster (ET Cluster).

card.question: What is the farthest thing you can see with your own eyes?
card.glance: An elongated gray glow in Andromeda with a bright, star-like core, much longer than it is wide.
card.see: From Mirach, the middle bright star of Andromeda, climb two fainter stars to the north and the glow appears. The oval core is obvious, and with averted vision the haze stretches about three degrees, six Moon widths, with M32 as a fuzzy “star” just south of the core.
card.understand: Andromeda is a spiral galaxy much like our Milky Way, seen steeply tilted, so its disk is squeezed into an oval. For centuries it was a “nebula” of unknown distance, until Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in it in 1923, a pulsing star whose rhythm gives away its true brightness. How faint that star looked put Andromeda far outside our galaxy, and Hubble’s modern namesake telescope has since timed 55 of them.
card.answer: For most people it is this glow: hundreds of billions of suns whose light set out about 2.5 million years ago, before our species existed. You see the galaxy as it was when our ancestors were first shaping stone tools.
card.wonder: Andromeda is closing on us at about 300 km/s, and billions of years from now it and the Milky Way may merge into a single galaxy.
card.connect: Our own galaxy would look much like this from outside, with small companions of its own, like M32 here.

journeys.title: Carina, a Family Album
journeys.drivingQuestion: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters now?
journeys.hook: Stars are born in litters from one cloud, then slowly wander away from their siblings.
journeys.story: Somewhere in the galaxy the Sun's brothers and sisters are still out there, scattered beyond recognition. Tonight's star families show how that happens, starting with the Jewel Box.
journeys.payoff: Every star was born into a family, and most families slowly scatter; the Wishing Well Cluster shows one well along that road, and the Sun's own family went the same way long ago.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Carina

stops.name: Jewel Box

getThere.text: Find Mimosa by eye, one of the arms of the Southern Cross, about 55° up in the south-west. From there, hop left about 1° (a fraction of one field of your 6.5° binoculars) to the Jewel Box.

stops.whyHere: We begin with the Jewel Box, a family of stars that has not yet drifted apart.

card.question: Why does one star in the Jewel Box glow orange among blue-white siblings?
card.glance: A tight little group of bright stars beside Mimosa in the Southern Cross, with one orange star among the white.
card.see: Start at Mimosa, on the eastern arm of the Cross, and nudge just over a degree south-east. A compact clump shaped like a letter A appears, much smaller than the Moon, mostly blue-white with one distinctly orange star near the middle; defocus slightly to bring out the colors.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, roughly 16 million years ago, so the only big difference between them is how much mass each started with. A heavier star squeezes its core harder and burns its fuel disproportionately fast, so it runs out first. The heaviest member has already reached that point and swollen, while its lighter blue-white siblings carry on in their steady adult life.
card.answer: Born with the rest, it was the heaviest of the family and so aged fastest, swelling into a cooler, orange-red supergiant while its siblings are still in their prime.
card.wonder: Its brightest stars weigh 15 to 20 times the Sun, and their light has been traveling for about 6,400 years.
card.connect: Right beside it lies the Coalsack, a cloud of dust that has made no stars at all.

stops.name: Pearl Cluster

getThere.text: Move down about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (9°), and the Pearl Cluster is there, in Centaurus.

stops.whyHere: The Pearl Cluster is a young family a few tens of millions of years old, at a similar distance to the Running Chicken nursery.
stops.transitionText: The Pearl Cluster and the Jewel Box are compact young families at almost the same distance, about 6,400 light-years, the Pearl a few times older.

card.question: What does a star family look like ten times older than a nursery?
card.glance: A bright, compact knot of stars in the Centaurus Milky Way, smaller than the Moon.
card.see: It sits in a rich Milky Way field about one and a half degrees north of Lambda Centauri. Binoculars show a tight, bright clump with several stars resolved over a soft glow, and a dark sky and steady hands bring out more.
card.understand: These stars formed together roughly 40 million years ago. That is old enough for their birth cloud to be gone, but young enough that many hot blue-white stars remain. Next to it, the glowing nursery around Lambda Centauri is only a few million years old.
card.answer: It looks like the Pearl Cluster, about ten times older than the nursery next door, its birth cloud gone but many hot blue-white stars still shining, the stage that follows the glow.
card.wonder: Gaia counts more than 700 members drifting through space together, about 6,300 light-years away.
card.connect: The Running Chicken nursery, just south, is the before picture.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Southern Pleiades

getThere.text: From the Pearl Cluster, slide down about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (7°) to the Southern Pleiades, in Carina.

stops.whyHere: The Southern Pleiades is a young star family on our cosmic doorstep, and binoculars turn its handful of stars into dozens of siblings.
stops.transitionText: The Southern Pleiades is a young open cluster like the Pearl Cluster, and about the same age too, 41–52 million years against 29–73 million years.

card.question: What does the southern sky’s answer to the Pleiades look like?
card.glance: A naked-eye spray of bright blue-white stars around Theta Carinae, wider than the full Moon.
card.see: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula. The naked eye counts five or six, while binoculars show two or three dozen, mostly blue-white, spread across about a third of the field.
card.understand: These stars were born together from one cloud, and their blue-white color shows that the brightest are hot, heavy stars still in their steady adult life. Astronomers dated the family from its faintest, coolest members, which slowly destroy the fragile element lithium inside them. The dividing line between stars that still have lithium and those that have lost it works like a clock, and here it reads about 46 million years.
card.answer: A loose naked-eye spray of blue-white stars around Theta Carinae, about 491 light-years away, almost exactly as far as the Pleiades. If you know the northern cluster, the resemblance is striking, though this family is younger.
card.wonder: The light you see left these stars around the time Magellan’s ships first sailed through these southern skies.
card.connect: Its twin, the Omicron Velorum Cluster, lies west in Vela, at the same distance and nearly the same age.

stops.name: Wishing Well Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep right about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°) to the Wishing Well Cluster, still in Carina.

stops.whyHere: The Wishing Well Cluster is a family far along the road of drifting apart. The Wishing Well is one of the richest star families in the sky and far older than the Carina clusters, a difference you can see.
stops.transitionText: The Wishing Well Cluster is an open cluster like the Southern Pleiades, but about 300 million years old against 41–52 million years.

card.question: How does a star family change after 300 million years?
card.glance: A big, rich oval of stars, wider than the full Moon, about three degrees east of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains with darker gaps between, and a few yellow-orange stars sprinkled among the white ones.
card.understand: This family is about 300 million years old, so its heaviest stars have already lived and died. Astronomers confirmed which stars belong by combining a decade of speed measurements with Gaia’s tracking of their motion across the sky, a census of hundreds of true members. Its brightest survivors are white stars, and the few that have swollen into orange giants are those just a little heavier than the rest.
card.answer: Its heaviest blue stars die first, leaving white stars and a few orange giants as the brightest members. Compared with the blue-white youngsters around the Carina Nebula, it is the same kind of family many chapters later.
card.wonder: It holds thousands of stars, yet it is slowly coming apart, and in time its stars will drift off into the galaxy.
card.connect: The Carina Nebula next door holds families so young they are still wrapped in their birth cloud.

journeys.title: Crux Under a Bright Moon
journeys.drivingQuestion: What can you still see when the Moon floods the sky?
journeys.hook: A bright Moon is no enemy of star colors and double stars, which it cannot wash out.
journeys.story: Moonlit nights have their own treasures. Starting with Alpha Centauri, tonight's stops were chosen to shine through the glare, and each holds up well in it.
journeys.payoff: Plenty survives moonlight, star colors, double stars and bright families of stars among it, with the Jewel Box as tonight's proof.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south, around Crux

stops.name: Alpha Centauri
stops.plainClass: yellow star + orange dwarf + red dwarf

getThere.text: Find Alpha Centauri by eye, the brighter of the two Pointers beside the Southern Cross, in Centaurus, about 60° up in the south. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The Moon washes out the faint things tonight, but Alpha Centauri is bright and colorful enough to shine straight through.

card.question: What is the nearest star system you can see with the naked eye?
card.glance: The outer of the two bright Pointers beside the Southern Cross, in Centaurus, a single dazzling yellow-white point.
card.see: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show one brilliant point, because its two Sun-like stars sit too close to separate without a telescope. Compare its warm tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
card.understand: Its distance was among the first ever measured, by parallax: as Earth swings around the Sun, a near star shifts slightly against the far ones, and the smaller the shift, the farther the star. Alpha Centauri’s shift is the largest of any naked-eye star, under a second of arc, about the width of a coin seen from several kilometers. Behind that one point are two stars circling every 80 years, one nearly a twin of our Sun and one a smaller orange star.
card.answer: Alpha Centauri, whose light takes about 4.4 years to reach you. Its faint third member, the red dwarf Proxima, is closer still, the nearest single star of all.
card.wonder: If the Sun were a 1 cm marble, Earth would be a grain of sand a meter away, and Alpha Centauri another marble about 300 km away.
card.connect: Hadar, the other Pointer, looks almost as bright yet belongs to a completely different league of stars.

stops.name: Mimosa

getThere.text: From Alpha Centauri, slide down and to the right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (14°) to Mimosa, in Crux.

stops.whyHere: Mimosa is a hot young star with a star cluster of the same age sitting right beside it in the sky. Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.
stops.transitionText: One is old and one is young, about 4.9 billion years for Alpha Centauri against about 16 million years for Mimosa.

card.question: Can a star and a cluster born at the same time sit side by side?
card.glance: The eastern arm of the Southern Cross, a blue-white star and your signpost to the Jewel Box.
card.see: Mimosa is the bright blue-white star on the Cross’s eastern arm. Place it at the edge of your view and look about 1° south-east, where a tight, glittering knot of stars appears: the Jewel Box, whose brightest stars share Mimosa’s icy color.
card.understand: Mimosa is a heavy, hot star that swells and shrinks very slightly several times a day, too little for your eye to notice. Its motion through space suggests it belongs to a scattered family of stars born together about 16 million years ago. The Jewel Box is dated separately, from its own brightest stars, and lands at a similar age.
card.answer: They can, for Mimosa and the Jewel Box are both about 16 million years old, yet the Jewel Box lies more than twenty times farther away: the same birthday at very different addresses.
card.wonder: You hold two families of the same age in one binocular view, one spread across the sky around you and one packed into a distant jewel.
card.connect: Gacrux, the orange star at the top of the Cross, is the one star here that does not belong with the others.

stops.name: Gacrux

getThere.text: No hop needed: Gacrux sits in the same view, below and to the right of Mimosa.

stops.whyHere: Gacrux looks like part of the Cross’s family, but it is a stranger, a nearby red giant that only lines up with the others.
stops.transitionText: Mimosa is a hot young blue-white star and Gacrux a cool orange giant near 3,700 K, which makes the swing between them a lesson in color.

card.question: Why is the top star of the Southern Cross orange when the others are blue-white?
card.glance: The top of the Southern Cross, the only orange star in a blue-white pattern.
card.see: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange with blue-white Acrux at the foot; defocus slightly and the color jumps out. A faint white star just to the north-east is a chance background star, not a partner.
card.understand: Gacrux is a red giant, a star that has used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen to about 80 times the Sun’s width. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 K, which is why it glows orange-red. Its parallax is several times larger than those of the other Cross stars, which places it much nearer to us.
card.answer: Gacrux is not one of the Cross’s blue-white family at all: it is an old red giant three to five times closer than the others. The Cross is a family photo with a neighbor standing in front.
card.wonder: Its light set out less than a century ago, while the blue-white stars behind it sent theirs centuries earlier.
card.connect: Giants like this one end by puffing away their outer layers into a glowing shell, a planetary nebula, around a hot dying core.

stops.name: Acrux

getThere.text: From Gacrux, slide down and to the left about one field of your 6.5° binoculars (6°) to Acrux, still in Crux.

stops.whyHere: Acrux is the brightest star of the Southern Cross and the place to ask whether the Cross is a family or a coincidence.
stops.transitionText: Acrux and Gacrux share a constellation but not a neighborhood, one at about 320 light-years and the other at about 89.

card.question: Do the stars of the Southern Cross really belong together?
card.glance: The foot of the Southern Cross, a dazzling blue-white point with a fainter star beside it.
card.see: Acrux is the bright star at the bottom of the Cross, and binoculars show a much fainter star beside it. The two brilliant stars that make up Acrux itself sit too close for binoculars, though a small telescope splits them.
card.understand: Stars born together drift through space together, so astronomers test family ties by measuring each star’s motion across the sky and its distance. Delta Crucis, and probably Mimosa, share the motion of a scattered family of hot young stars called an association. Acrux seems to belong too, though its measured motion fits less neatly, and the debate continues.
card.answer: Mostly they do: Acrux probably shares a scattered family born about 16 million years ago with Mimosa and Delta Crucis, while orange Gacrux, at the top, is a nearer stranger that only lines up with them.
card.wonder: The brighter of the two stars inside Acrux is itself a pair that only its spectrum reveals, so this one point of light holds at least three stars.
card.connect: Swing up to Gacrux at the top of the Cross and compare the colors: a blue-white family and an orange stranger.

stops.name: Jewel Box

getThere.text: No hop needed: the Jewel Box sits in the same view, above and to the right of Acrux.

stops.whyHere: The Jewel Box is the last of tonight's moonproof sights. It is a young star family with one member already turned red, a heavy star’s fast life written in color.
stops.transitionText: The Jewel Box shares this patch of sky with Acrux, yet it is about 20 times farther, a trick of perspective.

card.question: Why does one star in the Jewel Box glow orange among blue-white siblings?
card.glance: A tight little group of bright stars beside Mimosa in the Southern Cross, with one orange star among the white.
card.see: Start at Mimosa, on the eastern arm of the Cross, and nudge just over a degree south-east. A compact clump shaped like a letter A appears, much smaller than the Moon, mostly blue-white with one distinctly orange star near the middle; defocus slightly to bring out the colors.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, roughly 16 million years ago, so the only big difference between them is how much mass each started with. A heavier star squeezes its core harder and burns its fuel disproportionately fast, so it runs out first. The heaviest member has already reached that point and swollen, while its lighter blue-white siblings carry on in their steady adult life.
card.answer: Born with the rest, it was the heaviest of the family and so aged fastest, swelling into a cooler, orange-red supergiant while its siblings are still in their prime.
card.wonder: Its brightest stars weigh 15 to 20 times the Sun, and their light has been traveling for about 6,400 years.
card.connect: Right beside it lies the Coalsack, a cloud of dust that has made no stars at all.

journeys.title: Scorpius, Seen as It Was
journeys.drivingQuestion: How old is the light landing in your eye right now?
journeys.hook: Looking farther means looking back in time, and each stop tonight shows older light.
journeys.story: Light is fast but not instant, so everything you see in the sky is already history. Each stop tonight shows older light than the last, from Zubenelgenubi out to the Sagittarius Cluster.
journeys.payoff: The light from the Sagittarius Cluster set out about 11,000 years ago, the oldest of the night, and it reached your eye in the same moment as the far younger light of Zubenelgenubi.
journeys.difficultyReason: HD 140283 is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the east, around Scorpius

stops.name: Zubenelgenubi

getThere.text: Find Zubenelgenubi by eye, the southern pan of Libra, the Scales, about 70° up in the north. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: The light you see from Zubenelgenubi left it around 1951, and each stop after it shows older light still.

card.question: Do two stars that look close really travel together?
card.glance: Libra's southern claw: a bright white star with a fainter companion clearly separate in any binoculars.
card.see: Find Libra between Virgo's Spica and Antares. Center Zubenelgenubi and look just north-west, where a fainter star stands clearly apart, about an eighth of a Moon-width away; it is easy even at 7×, and the bright star is white, the companion a touch creamier.
card.understand: To test a pair, astronomers check whether both stars sit at the same distance and drift across the sky together. These do: both are about 76 light-years away and moving side by side. The brighter star is itself a tight pair that only its spectrum reveals.
card.answer: These two do, though at a stately pace: their gap is more than 5,000 times the Earth–Sun distance, so one orbit, if they complete one at all, would take well over a hundred thousand years.
card.wonder: From either star, the other would shine far brighter than any star in our sky, yet still as a single point.
card.connect: Zubeneschamali, the other claw nine degrees north-east, is the star some call green.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the α Librae field; the companion is the fainter star to the north-west.

stops.name: HD 140283

getThere.text: From Zubenelgenubi, slide down and to the right about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (14°) to HD 140283, still in Libra.

stops.whyHere: Most nearby stars are the Sun's contemporaries, but a few are visitors from the Galaxy's youth, and HD 140283 is the most famous of them.
stops.transitionText: Zubenelgenubi is about 76 light-years away and HD 140283 about 200 light-years, another long step outward.

card.question: How old can a star in our own neighborhood be?
card.glance: A faint, unremarkable point in western Libra that needs a careful hop: one of the oldest stars you will ever see.
card.see: Hop about six and a half degrees east of Zubeneschamali (β Librae) and use the chart to pick out a faint, slightly yellow point among similar stars. There is nothing special to see; the wonder is in knowing what it is.
card.understand: Its atoms are a birth certificate: it holds only about a 250th of the Sun's share of elements heavier than helium, so it formed before many generations of stars had enriched the Galaxy's gas. In 2013 Hubble measured its distance precisely, which fixes its true brightness, and models of how such stars age gave a first answer near 14.5 billion years, awkwardly older than the Universe. Better models and a measured radius later brought it down.
card.answer: About 12 billion years, give or take half a billion: HD 140283 formed when the Galaxy was young and nearly free of heavy elements. It moves fast on a long, tilted orbit through the halo, perhaps born in a small galaxy the Milky Way later swallowed.
card.wonder: When the Sun and Earth formed, this star was already more than seven billion years old.
card.connect: Globular clusters such as M4 gather stars of the same vintage in crowds.

stops.name: Antares
stops.plainClass: red supergiant + blue-white star, varies irregularly

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (19°) to Antares, in Scorpius.

stops.whyHere: Scorpius is one big family of stars born about 11 million years ago, and Antares is the sibling that has raced ahead to old age.
stops.transitionText: From HD 140283 at about 200 light-years the view reaches out to Antares at about 470–670 light-years, about 3 times farther.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine it tens of thousands of times?
card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster beside it.
card.see: Antares glows low in the south as the red heart of Scorpius. Put it near the edge of the field and its orange deepens, especially if you defocus slightly; about two and a half Moon-widths to the west sits M4, a soft round gray glow.
card.understand: Antares was born perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, and heavy stars burn their fuel recklessly fast, so it has already used up its core hydrogen and swollen into a supergiant. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 degrees against the Sun's 5,800, which is why it glows orange-red. In 2017 astronomers mapped gas rising and sinking across that vast surface.
card.answer: Antares wins by sheer size: about 680 times wider than the Sun, so although each patch of its surface is dimmer than the Sun's, the total comes to tens of thousands of Suns. Swap it for the Sun and its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mars.
card.wonder: Antares is heavy enough to end as a supernova, probably within the next hundred thousand years or so.
card.connect: τ Scorpii, two degrees away, is a sibling still hot and blue.

image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph of the Antares field; the globular cluster M4 sits just to the west.

stops.name: Butterfly Cluster

getThere.text: Sweep down and to the right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (16°) to the Butterfly Cluster, still in Scorpius.

stops.whyHere: M6 is a family in early adulthood, about 50 million years old, and one of its members has already grown old.
stops.transitionText: The Butterfly Cluster lies about 1,470 light-years away, about 3 times farther than Antares.

card.question: Why is one star in this young cluster orange?
card.glance: A bright, scattered cluster shaped like a butterfly with open wings, an orange star on one wingtip.
card.see: From Shaula, the stinger of Scorpius, go about five degrees north. M6 fills a modest part of a 7° field, two loose wings spreading from a central body, and on one wingtip BM Scorpii glows clearly orange among blue-white members; defocus slightly to make the color pop.
card.understand: All these stars were born together, so the orange one is a sibling of the blue-white ones, only heavier. Heavier stars squeeze their cores harder, burn faster and run out of core hydrogen first, then swell into cool, luminous giants. In a family this age only the most massive members have got that far, so that single orange star is a timestamp.
card.answer: It was the heaviest sibling: BM Scorpii ran out of core hydrogen first and swelled into an orange giant, and its stage of life dates M6 at about 50 million years.
card.wonder: BM Scorpii is restless, slowly brightening and fading over roughly two years.
card.connect: M7, a few degrees south-east, is bigger, brighter and older.

stops.name: Sagittarius Cluster

getThere.text: Move down about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (15°), and the Sagittarius Cluster is there, in Sagittarius.

stops.whyHere: With the Sagittarius Cluster you reach deepest into the past. M22 is one of the nearest and brightest globular clusters, a city of stars from the Milky Way's youth, and probably the first globular anyone ever found.
stops.transitionText: The Sagittarius Cluster sits about 10,800 light-years away, about 7 times farther than the Butterfly Cluster, so its light has a longer road behind it.

card.question: What does an ancient city of stars look like up close?
card.glance: A big, round, bright ball of light just above the Teapot's lid, one of the best globular clusters in binoculars.
card.see: From Kaus Borealis, the top of the Teapot's lid, move about two and a half degrees north-east. M22 is a bright, slightly oval glow, brighter in the middle and fading smoothly outward; brace the binoculars and compare it with nearby M28, the same kind of object with a very different apparent size.
card.understand: A globular cluster is a tight swarm of hundreds of thousands of stars held by their own gravity. These formed about 12.5 billion years ago and orbit high above and below the Galaxy's disk. The big, short-lived stars burned out long ago, so what shines now are old red giants and stars like the Sun.
card.answer: It looks like M22, a bright, round glow whose edges begin to break into separate suns in binoculars, the first hint of the crowd inside. Abraham Ihle stumbled on it in 1665 while following Saturn.
card.wonder: Radio astronomers found two black holes in it, each roughly 10 to 20 times the Sun's mass, remains of its first, heaviest stars.
card.connect: M54, a few hops south, is a globular that came from another galaxy.

journeys.title: Reading the Heat of Scorpius by Eye
journeys.drivingQuestion: Is a red star hotter or cooler than a blue one?
journeys.hook: A star's color is its temperature, and your eyes can read it like a thermometer.
journeys.story: A star's color is a direct reading of its surface temperature, no instrument needed. Tonight's stops climb from cool toward hot, so compare each color with the last.
journeys.payoff: Stars differ in color because their surfaces differ in temperature, cool ones orange-red like Antares and the hottest blue-white like Shaula, just as a heated poker goes from red to white.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Scorpius

stops.name: Antares
stops.plainClass: red supergiant + blue-white star, varies irregularly

getThere.text: Find Antares by eye, the red heart of Scorpius, about 65° up in the east. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Tonight the stars are a thermometer, and Antares, glowing like an ember, sits at its cool end.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine it tens of thousands of times?
card.glance: The orange-red heart of Scorpius; in binoculars a vivid ember with a faint round globular cluster beside it.
card.see: Antares glows low in the south as the red heart of Scorpius. Put it near the edge of the field and its orange deepens, especially if you defocus slightly; about two and a half Moon-widths to the west sits M4, a soft round gray glow.
card.understand: Antares was born perhaps 15 times heavier than the Sun, and heavy stars burn their fuel recklessly fast, so it has already used up its core hydrogen and swollen into a supergiant. Its surface has cooled to about 3,700 degrees against the Sun's 5,800, which is why it glows orange-red. In 2017 astronomers mapped gas rising and sinking across that vast surface.
card.answer: Antares wins by sheer size: about 680 times wider than the Sun, so although each patch of its surface is dimmer than the Sun's, the total comes to tens of thousands of Suns. Swap it for the Sun and its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mars.
card.wonder: Antares is heavy enough to end as a supernova, probably within the next hundred thousand years or so.
card.connect: τ Scorpii, two degrees away, is a sibling still hot and blue.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

stops.name: Alniyat

getThere.text: No hop needed: Alniyat sits in the same view, above and to the left of Antares.

stops.whyHere: Alniyat sits right beside Antares, a sibling of the same age that has taken a completely different path.
stops.transitionText: σ and Antares were born in the same Upper Scorpius family, yet one is still blue-white and the other has already turned red, because heavier stars age faster.

card.question: How different can two stars of the same family look?
card.glance: A blue-white star two degrees west-north-west of Antares, with M4 between them.
card.see: Put Antares at the edge of the field and look two degrees west-north-west for σ. M4's soft glow lies about a degree south-east of σ, between the two stars.
card.understand: σ Sco is a hot giant of the Upper Scorpius family that gently pulses about four times a day, changing by only a few hundredths of a magnitude. Antares was born heavier and has already swollen into a red supergiant. σ, lighter, is still blue-white.
card.answer: Blue-white σ Scorpii and orange-red Antares share a family and an age, yet look like strangers, because they differ in mass and therefore in stage of life.
card.wonder: A faint companion 20 arcseconds away is within reach of steady, mounted binoculars.
card.connect: Antares beside it: same family, same age, opposite colors.

stops.name: Fang

getThere.text: No hop needed: Fang sits in the same view, just above Alniyat.

stops.whyHere: π Scorpii is another hot sibling of the Upper Scorpius family, and the yardstick for δ's wandering brightness.
stops.transitionText: Fang and Alniyat grew up in the same nursery.

card.question: Which star anchors the bottom of the Scorpion's head?
card.glance: The lowest of the three stars in Scorpius' head; a blue-white point.
card.see: π is the bottom star of the short arc formed with δ and β. Use it, with β, as a brightness yardstick for δ, whose light wanders.
card.understand: π Sco is a close pair of hot young stars, too tight for any telescope to split, revealed only by the way their spectral lines shift back and forth. Both belong to the Upper Scorpius group, about 11 million years old. Its own light barely flickers, which makes it a steady reference.
card.answer: Fang, the lowest star of the head: a hot young pair that holds steady, the perfect yardstick for wandering δ.
card.wonder: Its light has been traveling for about six centuries.
card.connect: δ, just above, may now be the brighter of the two.

stops.name: μ¹ Scorpii
stops.plainClass: pair of blue-white stars, eclipsing binary

getThere.text: From Fang, slide right about two and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (16°) to μ¹ Scorpii, still in Scorpius.

stops.whyHere: Some stars change because of what happens inside them and some because of the company they keep, and μ¹ Scorpii is two stars so close they almost touch.
stops.transitionText: Fang and μ¹ Scorpii are siblings, born from the same cloud at about the same time.

card.question: What makes a star dip in brightness every day and a half?
card.glance: A naked-eye pair of blue-white stars in the curl of Scorpius' tail; the brighter one quietly dips every day and a half.
card.see: Follow the tail of Scorpius down from Antares to where it starts to curl. μ¹ and μ² sit about a fifth of a Moon-width apart, a naked-eye pair that binoculars widen into two blue-white points; use μ² as your yardstick, since some nights μ¹ looks clearly brighter and others almost equal.
card.understand: μ¹ is two hot stars whirling around each other every 35 hours, so close that one has swollen to fill its share of space and spills gas onto its partner. We see the orbit nearly edge-on, so on every lap each star passes in front of the other. Astronomers call this an eclipsing binary, and its light curve is a record of the orbit.
card.answer: Eclipses do it, for on every orbit each star blocks part of the other and the combined light dips by about a fifth.
card.wonder: To complete an orbit in about a day and a half, their surfaces race along at hundreds of kilometers per second.
card.connect: Farther down the tail, ζ Scorpii is a naked-eye pair that is a complete illusion.

stops.name: Shaula

getThere.text: From μ¹ Scorpii, slide down about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (8°) to Shaula, still in Scorpius.

stops.whyHere: The scale tops out at Shaula, a blue-white star. Mass decides a star's whole life, yet you cannot put a star on a scale, and Shaula, the Scorpion's sting, is one of the systems that shows how it is done.
stops.transitionText: μ¹ and Shaula are both tight families of hot stars, and their orbits are how astronomers weigh them.

card.question: How do astronomers actually weigh a star?
card.glance: The bright blue-white stinger at the tip of Scorpius' tail, with fainter Lesath just beside it.
card.see: Follow the tail of Scorpius to its hook: the bright stinger is Shaula, with fainter Lesath just over half a degree west-south-west, both blue-white. Then sweep about five degrees north-east to the big, bright cluster M7.
card.understand: Shaula looks like one star but is at least three: two hot stars circling each other every few years, and a small third star whipping around the brightest every six days. Newton's law ties an orbit's size and period to the total mass inside it, so once you know how wide the orbit is and how long it takes, the mass follows. In 2006 an interferometer in Australia measured the wide orbit directly.
card.answer: Shaula's two main stars were weighed just this way, at about ten and eight Suns, from their motion around each other. The same orbit also gave the system's distance, which came out smaller than earlier estimates.
card.wonder: The brightest of the three also rings like a bell, swelling and shrinking slightly almost five times a day.
card.connect: M7, to the north-east, is a cluster so bright it was recorded in antiquity.

sides.role: Reading the Heat of Scorpius by Eye

conditions.message: The Moon is 100% lit and up. Its glow washes out faint nebulae and galaxies, so every stop is kept at least 40° from it; it sets at 07:52.

journeys.title: Puppis' Moonproof Wonders
journeys.drivingQuestion: What does moonlight leave untouched?
journeys.hook: The Moon steals the faint things tonight, so the night belongs to color and pairs.
journeys.story: Moonlit nights have their own treasures. Starting with Naos, tonight's stops were chosen to shine through the glare, and each holds up well in it.
journeys.payoff: Plenty survives moonlight, star colors, double stars and bright families of stars among it, with M47 as tonight's proof.
journeys.difficultyReason: M46 is a faint challenge stop; a dark sky and steady hands help.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Puppis

stops.name: Naos

getThere.text: Find Naos by eye, the brightest star of Puppis, the Stern, in the Milky Way south-east of Sirius, about 60° up in the south-west. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Moonlight cannot touch Naos, a blue-white supergiant bright enough to ignore the glare.

card.question: How hot can a star you see with your eyes be?
card.glance: A steely blue-white star in a rich Milky Way field in Puppis.
card.see: In binoculars Naos is a sharp, steely blue-white point among many fainter Milky Way stars. Swing about 10° west to Pi Puppis, a deep yellow-orange star, and you have both ends of the temperature scale in neighboring fields.
card.understand: A star’s temperature is written in its spectrum: certain atoms only show their lines when hot enough to lose electrons, and Naos shows lines of helium stripped of an electron, a sign of extreme heat. Naos is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with about 25 times the Sun’s mass. It pours out roughly 450,000 times the Sun’s light, most of it ultraviolet.
card.answer: About 40,000 K, nearly seven times the Sun’s surface temperature, and most of its enormous output is ultraviolet light your eyes cannot see. What reaches you is only the visible tail of a far greater glare.
card.wonder: It also races through space, probably thrown out of its birth cluster.
card.connect: Gamma Velorum, next door in Vela, shows what such a star becomes once its outer layers are stripped away.

stops.name: Pi Puppis

getThere.text: Sweep down about one and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (10°) to Pi Puppis, still in Puppis.

stops.whyHere: Pi Puppis is the cool end of the Puppis thermometer, an orange supergiant 10° from blue-white Naos.
stops.transitionText: Naos and Pi Puppis, ten degrees apart, sit at opposite ends of the thermometer, about 40,000 K against about 3,900 K.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun shine 11,000 times brighter?
card.glance: A deep yellow-orange star in Puppis with a faint companion close by.
card.see: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange, with a much fainter star just beside it, an easy binocular pair. Then swing about 10° east to Naos for the color contrast.
card.understand: Pi Puppis is a supergiant, a heavy star swollen in late life, with a surface near 3,900 K. Each square meter of a surface that cool gives out only a fraction of the Sun’s light. Its total light, measured across all colors and scaled by distance, still comes to about 11,000 Suns, leaving one way to balance the books.
card.answer: It must be vast, and it is, about 230 times the Sun’s width, so its sheer extent makes up for its coolness.
card.wonder: It is the brightest member of a loose young cluster scattered around it, which binoculars show as a sprinkle of fainter stars.
card.connect: Ten degrees east, Naos burns ten times hotter.

stops.name: τ Canis Majoris
stops.plainClass: blue-white supergiant + blue-white star, eclipsing binary

getThere.text: From Pi Puppis, slide right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (12°) to τ Canis Majoris, in Canis Major.

stops.whyHere: τ Canis Majoris is a knot of young, heavy stars so luminous that it outshines the entire cluster around it, NGC 2362.
stops.transitionText: Swing from Pi Puppis to τ Canis Majoris and compare the colors, about 3,900 K against 32,800 K, and your eyes are reading a thermometer.

card.question: How can one star outshine its whole cluster?
card.glance: A star sitting inside a tiny, sparkling cluster in Canis Major, south-east of Sirius.
card.see: Find τ Canis Majoris about 2½° north-east of Wezen, below and left of Sirius. In 10× binoculars a halo of faint stars surrounds it; at 7× the cluster may look like a soft glow around one bright star.
card.understand: τ CMa is a small group of very hot, very heavy stars, including a pair that eclipses every 1.3 days. Its cluster, NGC 2362, is only about five to seven million years old, an age astronomers read from its members: the faint ones are still settling down, while none of the heavy ones has yet burned out. Heavy stars are not just a little brighter than light ones but enormously so, which is why a handful can outshine all the rest.
card.answer: By gathering the heaviest stars in one spot: τ CMa gives out so much light that it reaches naked-eye brightness from about 4,000 light-years, and its cluster mates are faint by comparison.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 4,000 years ago, when the first written laws were being carved in Mesopotamia.
card.connect: Close by lies VY CMa, what a star this heavy becomes after a few million more years.

image.caption: Survey photo of the binocular field around τ Canis Majoris, 4° wide; τ Canis Majoris is the star at the centre, between the four marks. North up, east left. A long photographic exposure, so it shows more stars and colour than binoculars do.

stops.name: M46

getThere.text: Sweep right about two fields of your 6.5° binoculars (11°) to M46, in Puppis.

stops.whyHere: M46 is a rich, older cluster three times farther than M47, with a famous impostor in front of it. This is the night's challenge, and if it will not show after a patient minute, move on.
stops.transitionText: One is young and one is old, about 4.3–9.3 million years for τ Canis Majoris against about 270–690 million years for M46.

card.question: Does the little ring nebula in M46 belong to the cluster?
card.glance: A round, misty patch in Puppis about the size of the full Moon, with a few faint stars glinting in it.
card.see: From M47, move just over a degree east. In 10×50 binoculars M46 is a soft, even glow with a few stars at the threshold, and dark skies with averted vision resolve more; the little ring nebula NGC 2438 near its north edge is too faint for binoculars.
card.understand: M46 has more than twice as many members as M47, but at about 5,000 light-years its stars blend into a glow. The ring in front of it is the cast-off shell of a dying star, a planetary nebula. Measuring speeds settled the question: the nebula moves at a speed about 30 km/s different from the cluster’s, and the distance of its central star puts it much nearer.
card.answer: NGC 2438 is a dying star’s shell roughly half as far away, lined up with M46 by pure chance, so the tidy picture in the eyepiece hides two unrelated objects.
card.wonder: The ring is the shed skin of a star not unlike the Sun, a preview of what our own star will leave behind.
card.connect: Puppis is full of these depth tricks: NGC 2451 and NGC 2477 stack three families in one view.

stops.name: M47

getThere.text: No hop needed: M47 sits in the same view, below and to the left of M46.

stops.whyHere: M47 is the last of tonight's moonproof sights. It is half of the sky’s best side-by-side comparison, a near, young cluster next to a far, older one.
stops.transitionText: M47 and M46 are neighbors on the sky only, M46 about three times farther and about four times older.

card.question: Are two clusters side by side in one field really neighbors?
card.glance: A bright, loose cluster of a few dozen stars in Puppis, with its partner M46 in the same binocular field.
card.see: Center M47, a coarse scatter of bright blue-white stars about the width of the full Moon, easy even from the suburbs. Then look just over a degree east for M46, a fainter, finer, misty patch, and keep both in one field to compare their sparkle and texture.
card.understand: M47 is roughly 100 million years old, and its brightest stars are still hot and blue-white. Gaia measures the parallax of more than 1,100 of its members, and averaging them gives a precise distance of about 1,500 light-years. The same method puts M46 about three times farther.
card.answer: M47 is near and young, while M46 beside it is about four times older and more than 3,500 light-years behind. Distance dims M46’s stars into a mist, and age has taken away its brightest blue ones.
card.wonder: Messier logged M47 with a slip in its position, and for nearly two centuries nobody could say which cluster he had meant.
card.connect: M46, a degree east, shows what more distance and more time do to a star family.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph (DSS2): the bright, sparse cluster.

journeys.title: Carina, Pair by Pair
journeys.drivingQuestion: If two stars look alike, why do they live such different lives?
journeys.hook: Neighbors on the sky can be worlds apart in age, size or distance.
journeys.story: Two stars can share a patch of sky, a color or a brightness and still be strangers. Tonight's game is finding the hidden fact that sets each pair apart.
journeys.payoff: One hidden property, whether temperature, age, distance or mass, set each pair apart even when they looked alike, and the Wishing Well Cluster showed how wide that gap can be.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the south-east, around Carina

stops.name: Delta Velorum
stops.plainClass: two white stars + yellow-white star, eclipsing binary

getThere.text: Find Delta Velorum by eye, a corner of the False Cross, in Vela, about 65° up in the south-west. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Delta Velorum is the first of tonight's look-alikes, easy to find and less simple than it appears.

card.question: How could a bright star hide its eclipses for all of history?
card.glance: One corner of the False Cross, a bright white star that dims for some hours every few weeks.
card.see: Find the False Cross in Vela and Carina, a larger, fainter look-alike of the Southern Cross, and Delta Velorum is one of its four corners. On most nights it is clearly brighter than Kappa Velorum and Aspidiske, and during an eclipse it drops to about their level.
card.understand: Delta Velorum is two white stars orbiting each other every 45 days, and our view runs almost along their orbit, so once per orbit one passes in front of the other: an eclipsing binary. Each dip lasts only hours and costs less than half a magnitude, so in most years you would have to be watching at just the right time. An amateur caught one by eye in 1997, and the star-tracker of NASA’s Galileo probe, which used the star to steer, had recorded others.
card.answer: Its eclipses are rare and brief, one short dip per orbit, and they slipped past generations of observers until 2000, when the two records were put together. Even the brightest stars can keep a secret.
card.wonder: A spacecraft on its way to Jupiter noticed what astronomers on Earth had missed.
card.connect: The False Cross fools navigators, and its stars are not even close together: Avior is roughly seven times farther away.

stops.name: Theta Carinae

getThere.text: Sweep left about two and a half fields of your 6.5° binoculars (18°) to Theta Carinae, in Carina.

stops.whyHere: Theta Carinae is the leading light of a nearby star family, and its neighbor Eta Carinae turns brightness upside down.
stops.transitionText: Theta Carinae is about 230 times more luminous than Delta Velorum, whatever their brightness in your binoculars suggests.

card.question: Which looks brighter, a nearby cluster star or a distant monster?
card.glance: The brightest star of the Southern Pleiades in Carina, a scatter of blue-white stars that fills a binocular view.
card.see: Theta Carinae is the brightest of a loose group of blue-white stars visible even to the naked eye. In binoculars the group fills about half your view, with dozens of fainter members, and about 5° north lie the Carina Nebula and Eta Carinae.
card.understand: The Southern Pleiades, IC 2602, is an open cluster, a family of stars born together, tens of millions of years old and about 490 light-years away. Theta Carinae is its brightest and hottest member. Eta Carinae looks fainter from here, yet it is more than 15 times farther away, so it must be vastly more powerful.
card.answer: The nearby star wins to the eye: Theta Carinae, about 456 light-years away, outshines Eta Carinae, although Eta Carinae is the true giant, because apparent brightness always mixes power with distance.
card.wonder: Seen from a planet near Eta Carinae, this whole cluster would be too faint to notice.
card.connect: Swing north to Eta Carinae and compare: the fainter-looking star is the true giant.

image.caption: Survey photo of the binocular field around Theta Carinae, 4° wide; Theta Carinae is the star at the centre, between the four marks. North up, east left. A long photographic exposure, so it shows more stars and colour than binoculars do.

stops.name: Eta Carinae

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: Eta Carinae is already in the same view, just above Theta Carinae.

stops.whyHere: Eta Carinae is one of the most massive and unstable stars known, and almost certain to end as a supernova one day.
stops.transitionText: Theta Carinae and Eta Carinae, five degrees apart, swap roles: the bright one is the near one, and the dimmer one is the monster.

card.question: What does a star on the brink of exploding look like?
card.glance: A small yellow-orange star buried in the bright Carina Nebula, whose brightness changes over the years.
card.see: Center the Carina Nebula, the brightest patch of the southern Milky Way. Near its brightest part sits a compact star with a warmer, yellow-orange tint than its white neighbors, and that is Eta Carinae. It looks ordinary; the drama lies in what it is.
card.understand: Eta Carinae is a pair of giant stars circling every five and a half years, and the heavier may once have weighed as much as 150 Suns. In the 1840s it blew off more than ten Suns’ worth of gas and survived, and that gas now forms a twin-lobed cloud, the Homunculus. Measuring how fast the cloud expands and how large it looks gives its distance, like judging a balloon by its growth.
card.answer: It looks surprisingly ordinary, a small yellow-orange point dimmed and reddened by the very cloud it blew off in the 1840s, and that quiet look hides a star that once nearly tore itself apart.
card.wonder: For a few years it was the second-brightest star in the night sky, even though its light travels about 7,500 years to reach us.
card.connect: Stars this heavy shed their outer layers before they die, and Gamma Velorum, in neighboring Vela, holds a star that already has.

stops.name: Gem Cluster

getThere.text: No hop needed: the Gem Cluster sits in the same view, above and to the right of Eta Carinae.

stops.whyHere: The Gem Cluster is a slightly older sibling of the Carina Nebula’s clusters, one whose birth cloud has nearly cleared.
stops.transitionText: The Gem Cluster shares a birth cloud with Eta Carinae, though the two have since moved apart.

card.question: What does a star nursery look like once its gas is gone?
card.glance: A small, bright knot of stars about two degrees north-west of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the bright heart of the Carina Nebula, move about two degrees north-west. Binoculars show a compact, bright clump much smaller than the Moon, with a few stars resolved around a hazy center.
card.understand: This family was born in the same great cloud complex as the Carina Nebula’s clusters, but several million years earlier. Hot young stars blow fierce winds and pour out ultraviolet light that pushes and boils away the gas around them, like sun on a morning fog. Here that work is nearly done, and the cluster stands in clear space.
card.answer: It looks like the Gem Cluster, a clean, bright knot of young stars whose hottest members have blown their birth gas away. Look from the glowing nebula to this cluster and you see the before and after of star birth.
card.wonder: Its light set out about 7,600 years ago, before the first cities rose.
card.connect: The Jewel Box in the Southern Cross is a near twin in age and distance.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photograph (DSS2): the compact cluster at the north-west edge of the Carina complex.

stops.name: Wishing Well Cluster

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: the Wishing Well Cluster is already in the same view, just left of the Gem Cluster.

stops.whyHere: With the Wishing Well Cluster, an open cluster, the night's last pair of look-alikes is complete. The Wishing Well is one of the richest star families in the sky and far older than the Carina clusters, a difference you can see.
stops.transitionText: One is young and one is old, about 9.7–23 million years for the Gem Cluster against about 300 million years for the Wishing Well Cluster.

card.question: How does a star family change after 300 million years?
card.glance: A big, rich oval of stars, wider than the full Moon, about three degrees east of the Carina Nebula.
card.see: From the Carina Nebula, move about three degrees east-north-east. Binoculars show dozens of stars in an elongated swarm, many in curving chains with darker gaps between, and a few yellow-orange stars sprinkled among the white ones.
card.understand: This family is about 300 million years old, so its heaviest stars have already lived and died. Astronomers confirmed which stars belong by combining a decade of speed measurements with Gaia’s tracking of their motion across the sky, a census of hundreds of true members. Its brightest survivors are white stars, and the few that have swollen into orange giants are those just a little heavier than the rest.
card.answer: Its heaviest blue stars die first, leaving white stars and a few orange giants as the brightest members. Compared with the blue-white youngsters around the Carina Nebula, it is the same kind of family many chapters later.
card.wonder: It holds thousands of stars, yet it is slowly coming apart, and in time its stars will drift off into the galaxy.
card.connect: The Carina Nebula next door holds families so young they are still wrapped in their birth cloud.

journeys.title: The Colors of Orion
journeys.drivingQuestion: Why do stars shine in different colors, and what are the colors telling us?
journeys.hook: In the sky red means cool and blue means hot, the reverse of every bathroom tap.
journeys.story: Red stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars the scorching ones, which surprises almost everyone. A gentle defocus makes the colors easier to judge, starting with W Orionis.
journeys.payoff: You have just read a thermometer stretched across the sky, from the ember glow of W Orionis to the blue-white blaze of Meissa, using only the color of their light.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-west, around Orion

stops.name: W Orionis

getThere.text: Find Orion’s Belt by eye, the row of three bright stars across the middle of Orion, about 55° up in the north. From there, hop down and to the left about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (8°) to W Orionis.

stops.whyHere: Tonight the stars are a thermometer, and W Orionis, glowing like an ember, sits at its cool end.

card.question: Why does W Orionis glow so warmly red?
card.glance: An orange-red star in western Orion, easy in binoculars.
card.see: Look about 7° south-west of Bellatrix, Orion’s western shoulder. Among white field stars it stands out as orange-red, and a slight defocus boosts the color.
card.understand: W Orionis is an old giant that fuses helium into carbon in a shell deep inside, and every so often its churning outer layers reach down and dredge some of that carbon up to the surface. In its cool atmosphere, about 2,700 K, the carbon forms molecules that soak up blue light. It also varies slowly in brightness, over about seven months.
card.answer: Carbon molecules in its cool atmosphere filter out the blue and leave a warm red glow, like a lamp seen through smoked glass.
card.wonder: Stars like this are a major source of the carbon in the galaxy, including the carbon in you.
card.connect: An even redder carbon star waits in Lepus, below Orion.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey 2 (POSS-II / UK Schmidt plates) · STScI / NASA; colour HiPS by CDS (Strasbourg), via the ESASky mirror; field reprojected by StarHop
image.license: DSS2: educational non-commercial use with acknowledgment
image.caption: Survey photo of the binocular field around W Orionis, 4° wide; W Orionis is the star at the centre, between the four marks. North up, east left. A long photographic exposure, so it shows more stars and colour than binoculars do.

stops.name: Alnilam

getThere.text: Sweep up and to the right about one field of your 7.1° binoculars (8°) to Alnilam, still in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Alnilam, the middle of Orion’s Belt, is a young blue supergiant that turns out not to be round.
stops.transitionText: One short swing takes you across the thermometer, from W Orionis near 2,700 K to Alnilam near 25,000 K.

card.question: How fast can a giant star spin before it starts to come apart?
card.glance: The middle star of Orion’s Belt, a brilliant blue-white point.
card.see: Center the middle Belt star and let the other two sit near the field edges. A curving string of fainter stars winds through the Belt, and many of them were born in the same burst of star formation.
card.understand: Alnilam is a blue supergiant, one of the biggest and most luminous kinds of star, about 28 Suns in mass. In 2025 astronomers measured its shape with the interferometer of ESO’s Very Large Telescope and found it is not round: its equator bulges outward, the signature of fast rotation. The same work gave a surface near 25,000 K and a distance of about 1,250 light-years, much closer than older estimates, which makes the star less extreme than once thought.
card.answer: Very nearly as fast as it can: though about 28 times wider than the Sun, Alnilam turns once in about four days, close to the point where its equator would start to fling gas away.
card.wonder: The much smaller Sun takes almost a month to turn once.
card.connect: Rigel, at Orion’s foot, shares the same blue-white color but sits a few hundred light-years closer.

stops.name: Alnitak

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: Alnitak is already in the same view, above and to the left of Alnilam.

stops.whyHere: Alnitak belongs to Orion’s young family of hot, heavy stars, and it is one of the few of its kind weighed directly rather than estimated.
stops.transitionText: Alnitak and Alnilam are siblings in the Belt group of Orion’s young family.

card.question: How do you weigh a star a thousand light-years away?
card.glance: The left-hand star of Orion’s Belt, brilliant blue-white.
card.see: Fit all three Belt stars in one field, then center Alnitak at the eastern end. Just south of it lies the Horsehead region, but binoculars show only stars there; the dark horse needs a telescope and a filter.
card.understand: Alnitak is a supergiant of the hottest kind, with a close partner that circles it every seven years. Astronomers followed that partner around a full orbit with an interferometer, which links telescopes to see fine detail, measuring how far apart the two appear on the sky, while spectra clocked how fast each moves toward and away from us. Put the angle and the speed together and you get both the true size of the orbit and the distance, about 960 light-years.
card.answer: You watch something orbit it, because the size and period of an orbit pin down the mass inside it, and for Alnitak they give about 14 Suns, oddly less than models of such a star had predicted.
card.wonder: Its light set out around the 11th century, when William the Conqueror crossed to England.
card.connect: Its Belt neighbor Alnilam looks just as bright, and it weighs about twice as much.

image.credit: ESO/J. Emerson/VISTA. Acknowledgment: Cambridge Astronomical Survey Unit
image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: VISTA's infrared view of the Flame Nebula beside Alnitak, the bright star at right. Infrared light pierces the dust that hides the nebula's young cluster from the eye; the Horsehead Nebula is the faint dark notch at lower right.

stops.name: Betelgeuse

getThere.text: From Alnitak, slide down and to the right about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (10°) to Betelgeuse, still in Orion.

stops.whyHere: Betelgeuse is what a heavy star looks like near the end of its life, a cool, swollen giant on Orion’s shoulder.
stops.transitionText: Defocus slightly as you move from Alnitak, at about 30,600 K, to Betelgeuse, at about 3,600 K, and the colors jump out.

card.question: How can a star cooler than the Sun outshine almost everything around it?
card.glance: A bright orange-red star on Orion’s shoulder, whose color blooms when you nudge the focus slightly off.
card.see: Betelgeuse marks Orion’s eastern shoulder, the bright orange star opposite blue-white Rigel. Turn the focus a little past sharp and the point blooms into a small disk whose orange-red suddenly becomes obvious; swing to Rigel to feel the contrast. Its brightness drifts over months, so judge it fresh each time.
card.understand: A star’s color is a thermometer, and Betelgeuse’s says its surface is only about 3,600 K, well below the Sun’s 5,800 K, so each square meter of it shines more feebly than the Sun’s. The surprise is how many square meters there are. Astronomers timed its slow pulsations and fed them into models of how heavy stars age, and out came about 18 Suns’ worth of matter swollen to some 760 times the Sun’s width.
card.answer: That is the whole trick: a dim glow spread over an almost absurd amount of surface still adds up to far more light than the Sun will ever give.
card.wonder: Put Betelgeuse where the Sun is and its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars.
card.connect: Heavy stars like this do not fade quietly, and the wreckage of one that already exploded lies next door in Taurus.

image.credit: ESO/M. Montargès et al.
image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: VLT/SPHERE images of Betelgeuse’s surface before (January 2019) and during the Great Dimming (December 2019 – March 2020).

stops.name: Meissa

getThere.text: No hop needed: Meissa sits in the same view, below and to the left of Betelgeuse.

stops.whyHere: Meissa sits at the hot end of tonight's thermometer. It is the hot heart of a young star family at Orion’s head, sitting in strangely empty space.
stops.transitionText: Meissa is about 10 times hotter than Betelgeuse, and the change of color as you swing between them is that difference made visible.

card.question: Where did the cloud that made Orion’s head go?
card.glance: The head of Orion: a tight little triangle of stars where you expect a single one.
card.see: Point at Orion’s head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn the faint naked-eye smudge into a compact triangle with a dozen fainter stars around it. The ring of gas shows only in long-exposure photos.
card.understand: Meissa belongs to the hottest class of stars and sits at the center of a young cluster called Collinder 69. Gaia’s measurements of more than a thousand members show a family about five million years old, all at the same distance. Around them lies a broken ring of gas and dust, and when astronomers reconstructed the region’s history they found signs that a star near the center exploded as a supernova, the death of a heavy star, and drove the leftover gas outward.
card.answer: The fierce light of its hot young stars, and probably that supernova, swept the leftover gas outward into a huge ring, leaving this family standing in the open.
card.wonder: The ring of gas this family blew outward is so wide that, in long-exposure photographs, it frames the whole head of Orion.
card.connect: Down in Orion’s Sword, a younger family is still wrapped in its cloud.

journeys.title: Orion's Hidden Pairs
journeys.drivingQuestion: When you see one star, how many are really there?
journeys.hook: Some pairs are bound by gravity and others are strangers lined up by chance.
journeys.story: Your eye sees one point of light, binoculars sometimes see two, and physics often finds more. From Sirius to Mintaka, tonight is an exercise in counting stars that hide behind one another.
journeys.payoff: Your eye counted one star, binoculars and physics counted more, and Mintaka is the proof that a single point of light can be a crowd.
journeys.difficultyReason: β Monocerotis is faint or tricky to find.
journeys.regionLabel: High in the north-east, around Orion

stops.name: Sirius

getThere.text: Find Sirius by eye, the brightest star in the night sky, in Canis Major, about 70° up in the north-east; Orion’s Belt points to it. Then raise your binoculars onto it.

stops.whyHere: Count the stars of Sirius by eye, then count again in the binoculars, because the difference is tonight's whole subject.

card.question: Why is Sirius the brightest star in the night sky?
card.glance: A blazing white point below and left of Orion’s Belt, flashing color when low.
card.see: Orion’s Belt, followed down and to the left, points straight at Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers red, green and blue, but that is our turbulent air, not the star. Park it near the edge of the binocular field to tame the glare, which also hides its faint companion.
card.understand: Sirius has about twice the Sun’s mass and a surface near 9,900 K, so it burns pure white, but plenty of stars are hotter and heavier. What sets it apart is its parallax: it shifts against the background more than almost any other bright star, which puts it only 8.6 light-years away. Every 50 years it is circled by Sirius B, a white dwarf, the bare cooling core a star leaves when it dies, and two decades of Hubble images of that orbit weighed both stars.
card.answer: Sirius is a fairly ordinary star that simply lives next door, so close that its light reaches you in under nine years.
card.wonder: Sirius B holds about a Sun’s worth of matter in a ball the size of Earth, so a teaspoon of it would weigh tons.
card.connect: Another winter star lets you see a white dwarf for yourself, with nothing more than steady binoculars.

image.credit: NASA, ESA, H. Bond (STScI), and M. Barstow (University of Leicester)
image.license: CC BY 4.0
image.caption: Hubble image with Sirius A deliberately overexposed so that the tiny white dwarf Sirius B shows as a dot at lower left.

stops.name: β Monocerotis
stops.plainClass: three blue-white stars, fast spinner with a gas disk

getThere.text: From Sirius, slide down and to the left about one and a half fields of your 7.1° binoculars (10°) to β Monocerotis, in Monoceros.

stops.whyHere: β Monocerotis looks like a single blue-white point, but it is a showpiece for small telescopes. The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.
stops.transitionText: Rank them by real output rather than by eye and Sirius gives about 25 times the Sun's light while β Monocerotis gives about 3,000 times the Sun's light.

card.question: Can binoculars show every star in a multiple system?
card.glance: A single blue-white star in binoculars, and a famous triple in a telescope.
card.see: β Monocerotis lies about 10° north-north-west of Sirius, in faint Monoceros. At 10× it looks single, but a small telescope at 100× splits it into a curved line of three blue-white stars.
card.understand: The three stars are only a few arcseconds apart (an arcsecond is a 3,600th of a degree), too close for binoculars, whose small lenses and low power cannot separate them. All three are hot blue-white stars, and they share a motion through space. The light reaching you left them about 690 years ago, and the three set out together.
card.answer: β Monocerotis keeps its secret from binoculars, looking single at 10×, and only a telescope reveals its three blue-white stars a few arcseconds apart.
card.wonder: Three stars of similar brightness in a tight line is a rare sight even in telescopes.
card.connect: σ Orionis, below Orion’s Belt, is a multiple that binoculars can split.

image.credit: Digitized Sky Survey · STScI / Caltech / UKST / AAO; color mosaic by CDS

image.caption: Survey photograph of the β Monocerotis field.

stops.name: Hatysa

getThere.text: From β Monocerotis, slide left about two fields of your 7.1° binoculars (13°) to Hatysa, in Orion.

stops.whyHere: ι Orionis, at the tip of Orion’s Sword, is a tight pair of stars with a violent past.
stops.transitionText: In the light they truly give off, β Monocerotis shines with about 3,000 times the Sun's light and Hatysa with about 510,000–970,000 times the Sun's light.

card.question: What flung two stars right out of Orion?
card.glance: The bright star at the bottom of Orion’s Sword, just south of the Orion Nebula.
card.see: The Sword ends in ι Orionis, just below the Orion Nebula. Binoculars show a scatter of fainter stars around it, the young cluster NGC 1980.
card.understand: ι Orionis is a close pair of heavy stars on a stretched orbit, an odd shape for so tight a pair and a hint of a violent past. Traced backward, the runaways AE Aurigae and μ Columbae both lead here, to about 2.5 million years ago. When two pairs of stars pass that close, gravity can swap partners and fling two of them away at high speed.
card.answer: Most likely ι Orionis itself, in a close brush with another pair that sent the two runaways off in opposite directions.
card.wonder: Two stars now on opposite sides of the sky were once neighbors here.
card.connect: One of the runaways, AE Aurigae, now sits far to the north in Auriga.

stops.name: σ Orionis

getThere.text: No hop needed: σ Orionis sits in the same view, just below Hatysa.

stops.whyHere: σ Orionis sits at the heart of its own young cluster below the Belt, and its stars are some of the best-weighed heavy stars known.
stops.transitionText: Underneath, Hatysa and σ Orionis share one idea. Many stars are two or more; some are true orbiting pairs, others are chance alignments.

card.question: How many stars hide in the single point of σ Orionis?
card.glance: A small knot of stars just south-west of Alnitak, the left-hand Belt star.
card.see: From Alnitak, drop about 1° south-west to a small knot of stars. At 10× σ Orionis shows a fainter companion to its east-north-east; a closer one due east, and many more, need a telescope.
card.understand: The central pair is far too close for any ordinary telescope, but interferometers, which link telescopes to see fine detail, have traced its orbit. Combine the size of that orbit on the sky with spectra that clock the stars’ speeds, and you get masses of about 17 and 13 Suns. The distance comes as a bonus, because the orbit’s true size in kilometers and its apparent size in arcseconds can only match at one distance.
card.answer: At least five stars are bound together here, and the central pair’s orbit pins the young cluster’s distance at about 1,260 light-years with rare precision.
card.wonder: Around the bright star swarm dozens of faint brown dwarfs, failed stars too small to burn hydrogen, born from the same cloud.
card.connect: The same young family stretches along the Belt just above.

stops.name: Mintaka

getThere.text: Don't move the binoculars: Mintaka is already in the same view, below and to the left of σ Orionis.

stops.whyHere: Mintaka is the last point of light to count tonight. Mintaka, the western Belt star, is a family of heavy stars whose distance has been surprisingly hard to pin down.
stops.transitionText: Mintaka runs on the same physics as σ Orionis, only in a different setting.

card.question: How far away is Mintaka, really?
card.glance: The right-hand star of Orion’s Belt, with an easy companion to its north.
card.see: Center Mintaka, the Belt star nearest Rigel’s side. Look about 50 arcseconds due north for a much fainter companion; binoculars split it with steady hands.
card.understand: Mintaka is a group of hot, heavy stars whose inner pair eclipses every 5.7 days, dimming it slightly. Satellite measurements of its parallax, the tiny yearly shift that gives distance, put it surprisingly close. But at that distance its stars came out too faint for their temperatures and masses, so astronomers turned the logic around and asked what distance makes everything consistent.
card.answer: About 1,380 light-years, roughly twice the satellite figure, which places Mintaka among its Orion siblings near the σ Orionis cluster.
card.wonder: Mintaka sits almost exactly on the celestial equator, so it rises due east and sets due west from anywhere on Earth.
card.connect: Its Belt neighbors belong to the same young family.
